items.title: A Reverse Ellis Island
items.description: Photographs by Lisette Poole J ulio Borrell knew he was being deported, but after 47 hours on a bus rattling through Mexico, he still had no idea where the United States was sending him. Through the window, he saw the cities give way to sprawling banana plantations and coffee farms. The passengers were still wearing whatever clothes they’d had on when they were detained by ICE: shirts splattered with paint from their most recent job, pajama pants, landscaping-company uniforms, bathing suits. Borrell had lived in Miami for 46 years. Now he watched as the bus passed a sign for the Guatemala border and then pulled over on the side of the road. “Where are we?” Borrell asked. “Tapachula,” a Mexican immigration agent answered. Borrell hadn’t heard of it. Neither had anyone else on the bus. The deportees weren’t from here. They weren’t even from Mexico. They were Cuban, Venezuelan, Nicaraguan, and Haitian—many of them elderly, some stripped of their green card after spending most of their life in the United States. The Trump administration, unable or unwilling to send them to their home country, had bused them 2,000 miles, from the U.S. border to a small city where they don’t have legal status. It’s a practice that started last year without any announcement and has quietly grown since then. “Why the hell did they bring us here?” Borrell, who migrated to Miami from Havana in 1980, asked me while I was in Tapachula this month. By the time we met, Borrell, a tall, sinewy 72-year-old with a shock of gray hair, had been in Tapachula for about six months, trying to make enough money fixing tires to rent a studio apartment. He knew that a handful of other Cuban deportees had been flown even farther away, to African nations such as Eswatini and South Sudan. But it was Tapachula that had become a mass waiting area for those rebuffed by U.S. immigration policy, out of sight of lawyers and human-rights defenders. This is now where the largest concentration of deportees is dropped in Mexico, and where most migrants traveling through Latin America en route to the U.S. are halted. Donald Trump can claim that the border is “closed” because it has effectively been relocated to Tapachula. The city looks and feels the way towns in northern Mexico along the U.S. border once did—a dumping ground for those expelled from the United States and a gathering place for those snagged on their way north. Mexican agents pull migrants out of commercial buses and cars on the freeway leaving the city, making sure the deportees don’t attempt to return to the United States. Another set of agents waits for the next busload of Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians to arrive so they can be processed. It’s what experts call externalization: the outsourcing of migration management to other countries. Julio Borrell, originally from Cuba, in Tapachula, on July 30, 2026 (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) Borrell told me that he’d come to the United States when he was 26 as part of the Mariel boatlift, the mass exodus of Cubans who traveled on crowded boats to Miami in 1980. He had seven American children, 11 grandchildren, and a great-grandchild. He had run a mechanic shop and renewed his visa each time it neared expiration. He could feel his body breaking down after years of physical labor and had been looking forward to retirement and more time with his family in South Florida. Then, last December, he went to his scheduled immigration check-in, as he had done dozens of times before. This time, he was detained by ICE agents. They sent Borrell to Florida’s Alligator Alcatraz for four months and then to Eloy Detention Center, in Arizona. From there, he was put on a bus for the U.S.-Mexico border and then another, bound for Tapachula. He walked on the side of the road for an hour before borrowing a cellphone to call his family back in Miami. “I’m in some place called Tapachula, Chiapas,” he told his daughter. Borrell, like thousands of other non-Mexicans deported here, arrived without clear legal status and with nowhere to stay. Many deportees sleep on the street for their first few nights. Mexico denies that it is facilitating deportations from the United States to Tapachula, even though more than a dozen migrants described to me the cooperation between U.S. and Mexican immigration agents in their expulsions. According to data from the Mexican Institute for Migration, 12,977 non-Mexicans were deported to Mexico from January 2025 to March 2026, largely to southern Mexico. They joined the tens of thousands of other migrants from all over the world who have been stranded in Tapachula during their journey to the United States, after being blocked by Mexican immigration agents from moving farther north. The mix of nationalities here has prompted officials at the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration to begin informally referring to the city as TapaYork—a kind of reverse Ellis Island. There are roughly 350,000 permanent residents of Tapachula and approximately 60,000 migrants living here. Some have tried to flee Tapachula multiple times, only to be deported back over and over again after being caught by Mexican agents. [ Read: The rushed, blundering effort to send deportees to third countries ] U.S. officials have consistently said that their goal is “zero border crossings”—a more absolutist project than Trump articulated during his first term, when it was easier for migrants to advance beyond Tapachula. This month, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that his department was accomplishing that goal. (Crossings are indeed way down, but they’re not at zero.) In meetings with their Mexican counterparts, U.S. officials continue to ask for more stringent immigration enforcement and accommodation for long-distance deportations, according to Mexican officials. The Mexicans, who fear unilateral U.S. military action, have generally complied. The Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians who are expelled here in buses that typically arrive a few times a week are evidence of Mexico’s acquiescence. In addition to the buses filled with foreigners, Tapachula’s tiny airport sometimes receives as many as five flights of Mexican deportees a day. (There have been more than 196 so far this year.) Most of the Mexicans arriving by plane head straight to the local bus station and return to their home state or to the border again. Some are minors and need to wait for their parents to pick them up. At the Tapachula airport, deportees arrive on flights from the United States. (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) In his first weeks here, Borrell, disoriented, was walking to an ATM to see whether he could withdraw cash when he saw a face he recognized. It was a Cuban friend from Miami, who ran a tile business. “What are you doing here, man?” Borrell asked. His friend, who had moved to the U.S. from Cuba when he was 6 and held a green card, had also been deported by bus. Borrell told him what he has said many times since: “We’ve got to get out of here. I’m not going to die in Tapachula.” F rom his small stand selling bread in downtown Tapachula, Mervil Wisdael, 43, sees the groups of deportees arrive a few times a week. “They’re lost,” he told me. “They’re just dragging their feet. They don’t even know where they are.” Wisdael, from Port-au-Prince, is part of a different population of migrants here, one that intended to pass through on the way to the United States. Tapachula has historically been a way station for migrants traveling north, including those who navigated the jungle of Panama’s Darién Gap before continuing to Mexico. I spent a week in Tapachula in 2018, when a caravan of migrants amassed there on their way north, early in Trump’s first term. Migrants slept in the central plaza, in the bus station, in rented rooms and shelters. It quickly became a media spectacle. Trump claimed that the group leaving Tapachula, which included many young Central American families, was full of criminals. He demanded that Mexico intercept them. A few days later, I walked with the migrants to the edge of the town, where Mexican immigration authorities had blocked the road. Hundreds of people were detained. Taking a break, one officer said to me, “We’re doing what your president asked.” Since then, the Mexican government has again and again bent to the will of the U.S. government on immigration enforcement. It signed off on the “Remain in Mexico” policy in 2019, which forced asylum seekers to wait for their immigration appointments from Mexico’s northern border rather than from within the United States. Under the Joe Biden–era CBP One program, it agreed to host asylum seekers even farther south, including in Tapachula. Then, during Trump’s second term, Mexico agreed to mass deportations to the city. Mexican officials told me that the main consideration for the Americans was Tapachula’s distance from the U.S. border and the way agents could create a choke hold on the only highway leaving the city. I came back to Tapachula to see how that series of capitulations had changed the city, a gritty commercial hub surrounded by miles of farmland, where near-daily afternoon storms briefly break the tropical heat. Read: A planeload of informants The refugee office in Tapachula often has a line outside as people seek residency in Mexico. (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) Wisdael had planned to make his way to the U.S. to reunite with his family and apply for asylum. But by the time he arrived in Tapachula, six years ago, Mexico was no longer allowing migrants to transit through the country without a humanitarian visa or refugee status, which could take months or years to get. He stayed until he got his papers, and then he waited longer to see whether it might get easier to cross the U.S. border. Many other Haitians stayed too. Roughly 10 percent of the city’s public-school students are now from Haiti. Each of its three semiprofessional basketball teams has Haitian players. The city’s market is peppered with stalls selling Haitian food. Employees of the municipal immigration office have taught themselves Creole. Wisdael has been in Tapachula longer than most of his countrymen. He speaks fluent Spanish. He met a Guatemalan woman, Ericka Leonardo, while working on a construction crew there. She was walking down the street. “You’re pretty,” he said. “I’ve never dated a Black guy,” she said. “Maybe you should try,” he said. They’re now married and live together in Tapachula. She works at an arcade around the corner from his bread stall. They’ve become informal sources of information about Mexico’s archaic immigration system. Wisdael explains to newly arrived Haitians that they need to line up at Mexico’s refugee office every 15 days so that a bureaucrat can sign a document proving that they have not absconded from Tapachula. After 30 or 40 or 50 signatures—anywhere from one to two years—most Haitians will have refugee status in Mexico. “They don’t want to wait that long. No one wants to wait that long here,” he said. Ericka Leonardo and her husband, Mervil Wisdael, at the arcade where Leonardo works, in Tapachula (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) But Wisdael knows that it’s not a good time to attempt to cross the U.S. border. Most people don’t even get that far. Haitians without Mexican papers are typically caught by Mexican immigration agents at a checkpoint just north of Tapachula. The city once felt like a stepping stone. Now it feels like a dead end . Almost every immigrant community in Tapachula has its own Wisdael—someone who has been around long enough to explain the rules to the newly arrived. Aside from the Cubans and Venezuelans, there are thousands of Central Americans, along with smaller groups of Congolese, Senegalese, Bangladeshis, and Nepalese. There’s a Cameroonian bar and a Ghanaian restaurant within walking distance of the 19th-century colonial church in the city center. The man guarding the door at one of the migrant shelters is Ukrainian. Most people have learned just enough Spanish to ask at least two questions: How long have you been here? And when are you leaving? Evening in Tapachula (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) B efore I left Tapachula, I was curious to meet the city employees running the municipal migrant-assistance center. I followed directions to a mostly abandoned covered market at the edge of town. I was sure I was lost. Then an enthusiastic 28-year-old, Kevin Figueroa, leapt out of his office holding a laptop. He had a PowerPoint presentation on migration in Tapachula. Did I want to see it? He flipped through the slides on the large numbers of migrant arrivals here and all of the ways the city had integrated them into municipal life. I knew that there had been protests over the past few years by locals upset about the way their city was changing. In 2022, Roberto Fuentes, the city council’s general secretary, told reporters that “the city is in a state of siege, a state of chaos.” At least once, Haitian street vendors like Wisdael have been physically removed from the city center by local police. But Figueroa assured me that Tapachulans had become accustomed to the way their city had been transformed. The economy was growing. The food was better. I partially believed him. In some ways, the city did seem to have settled into its new demographics. But there were still frequent confrontations between migrants and municipal employees—triggered, for example, by migrants using public electricity outlets to charge their phones. This month, several migrants set their mattresses on fire in the city’s migrant-detention center, leading the military to intervene. Two Venezuelans were arrested. Mexico’s immigration agency said obliquely in a press release that the protest was in response to “the dissatisfaction of a group of foreign nationals regarding their immigration process.” What seems to bother those trapped in Tapachula most is not the way they are treated in the city, but that they are here at all, in a no-man’s-land, far from any place they ever lived. It’s an approach the Trump administration plans to expand to more remote locations. Not long after I left Tapachula, the Liberian government announced that it would accept 1,200 non-Liberian deportees from the United States. Such an announcement would, until recently, have been a radical departure from decades of immigration policy. But there has been little outcry. The U.S. has kept the desperation of deportees and asylum seekers at a great distance. Some of the Cubans I spoke with in Tapachula told me that in the next week or two, they will begin marching north in their own migrant caravan. They know their chances of getting to the border are close to zero. But they think the effort might be enough to remind Americans that they are there, waiting at the southern tip of Mexico.

items.title: A Freedom 250 Event That Actually Worked
items.description: An interest in the thrills of car racing is not what drove me to spend my Sunday afternoon at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the latest of the spectacles that Donald Trump has presided over during the United States’ big birthday celebrations all summer. I was there yesterday because I was worried about art. The event involved 25 cars zipping around a number of D.C.’s museums and historic buildings at worryingly high speeds— 147 times . Preservationists and conservators had raised concerns ahead of the contest, leading me to imagine creaking sculptures and rattling ceramics, all because the president wanted a race around the National Mall. Seeing the National Gallery of Art’s huge black Alexander Calder sculpture outside, surrounded by wood boards as if the poor thing were hunkering down for war, didn’t help. But it turns out that playing art patrol is rather difficult at an IndyCar race, especially when you find yourself crammed into a sweaty crowd as blurs of color whiz by. This proximity to the action means you are a participant in a much more visceral way than at many other sporting events: You can feel the vibrations in your toes. Somewhere among the vroom s, I realized that this was not like the other Freedom 250 productions I had attended, like the Great American State Fair with its drab triumphal arch and the Freedom Trucks with their selective history. Instead, in some moments, the Grand Prix was … fun? The good vibes began when I spotted the driver Sting Ray Robb’s maintenance truck, decorated with the ridiculously wholesome image of seven puppies climbing on his race car. He immediately gained a fan in me, though he crashed early on. The course, with its many bumps, was tricky for drivers, and just more than half of them even finished. Kyle Kirkwood, another American, won. Many might be tempted to slot the IndyCar race next to other Trumpian events that have disrupted life in the nation’s capital. More than that, the race could easily serve as another example of how little an administration that has pressured museums and diluted historic-preservation laws cares for the nation’s cultural heritage. These interpretations aren’t overblown. Earlier this year, the Grand Prix unveiled (and later walked back) a disturbing T-shirt that featured a white-clad figure and read: One Nation One Race . In and around the city yesterday, the traffic was a pain for locals, the nearest airport had to stop flights for three hours, and the noise—including multiple deafening flyovers—was nothing short of a public nuisance. For those without tickets, access to the Mall was closed off. Madhan Subramanian, who lives by the course, told me he was “just a little annoyed by everything.” He thought it was a cool event, but “it was harder to get groceries and just do our normal thing.” The worries about vibrations and damage to artifacts were legitimate, too. In the middle of the race, I put my hand on the boarded-up geometric I. M. Pei skylights outside the National Gallery and found them shaking like a cellphone on vibrate. (Not great!) A man yelled to me over the thunderous cars, “Are we okay?” I replied, in earnest, “I’m not sure.” (So far, there have been no reports of damaged art.) Reckless is one word for what unfolded in the capital yesterday. But one person’s reckless is another’s exciting . And the Freedom 250 Grand Prix certainly had oomph to it. Trump did a lap of the track at the beginning of the race to the sound of mixed cheers and boos, and although I noticed Trump gear— Trump 2028 hats, for example—for sale outside the race perimeter, inside many fans had opted for checkers and race jerseys. In other words, this didn’t feel like another Freedom 250 event that was more about Trump than about America. Race-car driving occupies its own indomitable universe of fandom, kitsch, design, and hype. Ultimately, a race is a race, and many in the crowd appeared to be there simply for the sport. Keith Cole, a former amateur racer and F1 fan, was among them. A car race in downtown Washington seemed like a once-in-a-lifetime thing, so he came to D.C. with a friend despite some low-grade partisan energy they didn’t care for. “We don’t see a lot of people like us here,” Cole, who is Black, told me, noting some MAGA-hat sightings, too. “I understand how they want to use it to politicize it, but this is sports. You gotta, kind of, take it out of it.” Most of the time, the National Mall is a reflective space flanked by quiet, regal buildings that command a certain respect. Yesterday, though, America’s “front yard” felt more like a backyard. IndyCar fans played cornhole and giant Connect Four on the grass, which was dotted with lemonade stands and picnic tables. In one moment, I was surrounded by beer-drinking racing fanatics; in the next, I was engulfed in the smell of gasoline and the sound of revving engines; minutes later, after a short stroll, I was standing in the National Gallery in front of a Georgia O’Keeffe. Inside one of the galleries, I found Carol Madden—a native of Indianapolis, IndyCar’s namesake and the site of its premier event, the 500—seeking a break from the heat near some Renaissance-era earthenware. “The Indy 500 is Christmas for my family. We don’t come home for Christmas and Easter—we all come home for the race,” she told me. This was her 55th race, which she attended with her whole family, she said, getting teary-eyed. Nearby, Diana Vinson, as much a race-car fan as a museum lover, was immersed in a photograph on the wall. She didn’t see her appreciation for the two things as entirely separate. Both art and racing are all about precision; they’re about tiny decisions—in brushstrokes or tire pressure—that add up. “You have to understand your mediums,” she told me. The museum was making the most of any connection it could find with the event, which forced it to partially close for the race; the portion of it that remained open was accessible only to IndyCar ticket holders. (The National Gallery has been notably savvy about garnering attention of late, as evidenced by its viral videos of a Gen Z–whispering senior curator who called that Renaissance earthenware “bussin’.”) Outside, signs promised “iconic art (and air-conditioning).” Staff members had set up a tent where they sold T-shirts featuring a portrait of George Souders, who won the Indy 500 in 1927, from the museum’s collection. Earlier, out on the Mall, I had spoken with Bill Sherman, a fan of “anything that makes noise and goes fast,” who told me he thinks people are drawn to car racing because they can see themselves in it. “I’ve driven these roads hundreds of times,” he said. “It’s one of the few sports that you can look at and say, I can go out and do that every day on the Beltway .” Though that would certainly spice up your commute, you shouldn’t. Just like you shouldn’t send thousands of pounds of metal flying around historic sites. But watching cars hurtling past the National Archives, barreling toward the Air and Space Museum, with the U.S. Capitol looming in the distance, you might just convince yourself otherwise.

items.title: What a Bicentennial Baby Knows
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Thirteen seconds after midnight on July 4, 1976, Karen Steele was born in Montclair, New Jersey, and was anointed the first “bicentennial baby.” Newspaper articles followed. President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty, sent a note to the family. And then it kind of became a thing. Any baby born that year was treated like they had emerged playing the fife and drums. In Mobile, Alabama, new mothers received a commemorative blanket. In Covington, Louisiana, a hospital handed out (for $2.50) special “bicentennial baby” certificates on faux parchment, a “memento that can be framed and cherished as a family heirloom for endless generations.” This was a year of jaw-dropping kitsch , an explosion of red, white, and blue everything —toilet paper, lollipops, even condoms (pleading: One Time for Old Glory ). Branding newborns this way became part of the general patriotic fun. And although the tchotchkes surely ended up moldering in a red, white, and blue landfill somewhere, the label stuck. I know: I was one of those babies, born in August 1976. Being a bicentennial baby was not anything I ever thought about all that much. In fact, it was really only when meeting another person born in 1976 that it came up at all. Oh, you’re a bicentennial baby too , one of us would say to the other, smiling dumbly. This was a secret handshake that opened zero doors. But unlike other indelible parts of my identity that felt small in their particularity—like being the child of immigrants or being nearsighted—having my birth hitched somehow to the history of the country, to its forward motion, felt big whenever I was reminded of it. Beyond the horror of realizing that five of my current lifespans stacked up is all that separates me now from Benjamin Franklin, I’ve been thinking about this cohort of which I’m a part. Expounding on the significance of one’s own generation can lead rapidly to wild generalization, self-absorption, and some misplaced nostalgia. I know this. But I’m convinced that my fellow bicentennial babies and I have been through something unique. We’ve followed a distinct arc over the past 50 years: one of disillusionment. Better than most, we understand the disjunctions of our present because they happened at crucial inflection points alongside the timeline of our lives. We were born during a period of palate-cleansing. The Vietnam War was over. President Richard Nixon had, in 1974, resigned after Watergate, a redemptive scandal that renewed people’s faith in self-government. Journalists—yes, journalists —were sex symbols. Robert Redford played Bob Woodward in All the President’s Men . And the peanut farmer Jimmy Carter, a man who campaigned teeth-first, would be elected president in the fall, having promised a new era of idealism. [ Read: Inside America’s ugly birthday battle ] I don’t remember any of this, of course, but babies like me were launched into an atmosphere of reawakened good vibes. When Time magazine commissioned the polling firm Yankelovich, Skelly & White to gauge the country’s temperature from June to September of 1976, the company found a 10 percent jump in positivity on its “state of the nation index” between those months, the most rapid increase it had seen since it began tracking the metric. The following years were also a time of crime and stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, but at least by the indicators used by pollsters to determine collective mood, things continued to get generally sunnier into the ’80s. “The Zeitgeist has turned zesty,” Kurt Andersen wrote in a 1984 assessment of that year’s numbers. “The U.S. is at peace, and between rising employment and fading inflation, the economy is aglow. Americans are feeling more sanguine and comfortable about their country than they have felt in two decades. A rebirth of the American spirit, as Carter dearly hoped five summers ago? It sure feels like it.” I remember this optimism and confidence. On November 9, 1989, I sat watching television with my grandfather—a Holocaust survivor who that day, and most days, had his shirt off and a captain’s hat on his head. The Berlin Wall was coming down. This happened when we bicentennial babies were 13 and highly impressionable. Look at them , my grandfather said, his voice breaking, as people pick-axed their way out of East Germany. I recall the total elation on their faces when they finally broke through, and then the bracing thought that they were trying to get to the side where I already lived. The author in 1978 with his parents, sitting on his grandfather's Cadillac (Courtesy of Gal Beckerman) For many young Americans in those years, a feeling of transcendence was possible. You had a sense that good fortune had placed you somewhere that everyone in the world wished they could be. At the same time, that wider world, with its crumbling empires and ethnic cleansing and genocides, seemed very far away. Even the Gulf War of the early ’90s appeared, to those of us safe at home, as a ghostly green video game playing on CNN, transmitted from somewhere hard to recognize as real. You may not believe me when I tell you that I read Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History and the Last Man at 19, for fun, when I was a junior and living abroad in France . But I did, and then after college I went into the Peace Corps and lived in a village in Cameroon for two years. Although many of the people there thought that I was working for the CIA (I was not), I felt I was doing something uncomplicatedly wholesome, even a little patriotic. We were 25 when 9/11 happened. I moved to New York City in October of that year, like a salmon swimming upstream—or like a salmon following a girl. Everywhere were posters of missing people. During my first days of couch surfing, New Yorkers were further terrorized by anthrax spores sent through the mail, addressed to political and media targets. That terrible fall was a hinge moment for all Americans but maybe especially for us young adults, who were also at a hinge moment in our lives, suddenly vulnerable and less innocent in new ways, feeling silly for having believed that history could have an end. [ Jerusalem Demsas: The end of Francis Fukuyama ] I haven’t mentioned the internet yet, but it also came around for us as adulthood hit. I got my first email address in college and accessed my inbox in the library basement at a computer lab that perpetually smelled like Doritos. It was all so new that you could forget to send a paper to a professor and then offer the excuse that the email probably just got lost . I spent a lot of time outside that library, chatting, with nothing in my hands besides a cigarette. I think I knew someone who had a beeper. We got flip phones in our 20s. We were in our early 30s when the first iPhone arrived and Facebook showed up. We were told that these were revolutionary tools. Maybe we believed this more than other people did, still being relatively young and feeling like we were being handed powerful megaphones in our prime—a chance to make change, to connect. Then the tools congealed into yet more products that would waste our hours and make us feel terrible about ourselves and our fellow citizens. We made lives against the backdrop of distant wars, unceasing notifications popping up on our phones. The year we turned 40, Donald Trump was elected president. Four years later came COVID. Just as we were balancing more and more—perhaps children, a challenging job, ailing parents—the world seemed to conspire to keep our heads spinning. In these past few years, before we and the country hit our big milestones, we were assaulted by panicked warnings about the state of American democracy—and the future of the entire human race. What has AI been up to over the past few days? Creating new viruses and independently cyberhacking, it appears. We are less naive, though more exhausted. It has not been lost on us that the people warning that AI could lead to our extinction are the same people who invented it. This is a pattern we’re familiar with now: Technology gives us something with one hand while robbing us of something else with the other. I’m leaving out a lot. We also had private joys and tragedies totally impervious to what America writ large was up to. But I can distinguish a progression toward an increased sense of emergency, toward alienation, toward a mournfulness that makes me read the newspaper through my fingers most days. I don’t think this is the birthday blues talking—or, if I’m honest, maybe not just the birthday blues. It’s also the metrics: about loneliness and economic stagnation and political polarization and the whole insane technological surround sound of our lives. My point is that bicentennial babies, regardless of their individual circumstances, have all been strapped into the first row of this ride. Someone born on America’s centennial, in 1876, could well have argued that they had witnessed much more consequential change by their 50th birthday. They might have gushed about the expansion of railroads and telegraphs, about seeing the first airplanes, telephones, and radios, and then explained what it was like to face the reality that as many as 20 million people could be killed in a single war. I wouldn’t want to go head-to-head with them. Every generation has its story. But we bicentennial babies have lived through a major rupture. For all else that might be good in our lives—and I’m lucky to have a lot that’s good—this is not such an exuberant place to find ourselves at 50. [ Read: Trump’s 250th celebration is a fiasco ] Can we imagine anyone proudly calling the babies born this year—what? semiquincentennial sprouts ? A mouthful, granted. But that’s not what makes it sound strange. Behind the “bicentennial babies” moniker was a kind of hope. We would be the Americans of the future. And we would be moving toward that future not with dread but with anticipation. Whatever one’s political affiliation, people do not have much enthusiasm these days when they picture where we’re headed. When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans just before this year’s semiquincentennial, 59 percent of respondents said that the country’s best years were behind it. Asked to imagine the United States 50 years from now, 44 percent were pessimistic and only 28 percent were optimistic. Perhaps most telling, 27 percent chose neither option; they just felt blah . Recently, Conan O’Brian, speaking on the podcast The Rest Is History , talked about the “undiluted joy” he remembers feeling as a preteen experiencing the bicentennial. Now: “It’s very hard for some people, maybe, to just say, I’m really excited about our 250th when our current state is so divided .” I can’t conceive of myself being around for the tricentennial—and if I did suggest living to 100, my mother might faint from all the spitting she’d have to do to ward off the evil eye. But if I do make it there, I will have lived through a third of the country’s existence. I’ll have a lot more data to work with. Will 2026 appear in retrospect as another hinge, or simply as a snapshot of us—mouths open and eyes closed, as in an amusement-park photograph—mid–free fall? Will there be self-correction or a piling-on of bad decisions? Disintegration or newfound connection? No one can really tell. Though I do know what I would like on my 50th birthday and the country’s 250th: something for us to look forward to. ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: The Trump Comedians Are Tired
items.description: In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair —noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.” It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.” Clearly, something has changed—and not just for Baldwin, who effectively retired from the role back in 2020. The first Trump administration was a boon for comedians and for television. A cottage industry of new, politically inflected clip shows offered satirical commentary on the new president to a mostly liberal audience. Late-night comedy adopted Jon Stewart’s old playbook, trading quippy gags for more full-throated (and sometimes outright defiant) critiques of government. Ambiguity was out; everyone knew whose side these commentators were on, and other impersonators began vying for Baldwin’s crown. But the bubble collapsed right around the moment of Joe Biden’s ascension, and Trump’s return to power hasn’t inspired the same volume of riffs. Today, some of the comedians who rode the initial wave have come to feel a little like Baldwin does. They’re sick of the shtick—and they’re skeptical about the function of political comedy in a world that’s arguably beyond parody. [ Read: Why South Park did an about-face on mocking Trump ] Part of what once made Trump such a rich vein for comedic send-ups was that, at the start of his political career, he seemed straightforwardly ridiculous. Hadn’t this guy been shilling for Omaha Steaks with Gary Busey and Lil Jon? How would he spin the Oreo commercial he’d done with Peyton and Eli Manning, in which he’d challenged the brothers to a “lick race”? The jokes practically wrote themselves. Anthony Atamanuik, a Trump impersonator whose parody series, The President Show , ran for one season on Comedy Central in 2017, told me that at its best, the political comedy of that era also had a kind of diagnostic power: “I wanted my show to continue mostly because I saw each episode as an essay on an issue in American life, and the albatross I had was Trump.” His hope was that, for a liberal audience still reeling from the shock of his election, skewering the president could be a way to crystallize what had happened to the country. That initial burst of left-leaning satire didn’t last. Studios gave the former Daily Show correspondents Michelle Wolf, Larry Wilmore, Hasan Minhaj, and Wyatt Cenac their own shows, only to cancel them before the end of the president’s first term. A 2020 New York Times Magazine story on this “boom and bust” suggested that some comedians—and some audiences—were tiring of the material even before it became clear that Trump would lose the election. Network late-night shows continued to treat the president as a punching bag, but the novelty had worn off. Overexposure is one explanation for that decline. Another is that these liberal viewers started to expect something different from comedy as the reality of MAGA’s ascendance set in. More than over-the-top impersonators and Daily Show correspondents ridiculing the news, people seemed to be craving simple palliatives. By 2020, the most visible Trump satirist was the comedian Sarah Cooper, who filmed herself mouthing along to the president’s public statements while mimicking his facial expressions. Her work was almost post-comedic: Rather than writing her own material, she was giving people permission to laugh at the strangeness of his mannerisms. She eventually parlayed viral fame into a guest-hosting gig on Jimmy Kimmel Live and a Netflix special directed by Natasha Lyonne. Trump’s return to office in 2025 could have been an opportunity for any of these comedians to stage comebacks, or for new shows to emerge. But although the president remains a target in liberal comedy circles, the market for this brand of humor has shrunk considerably. It remains most evident in today’s late-night lineup: The Daily Show , one of the progenitors of the form, remains on the air. (Its original host, Jon Stewart, returned in 2024.) Last Week Tonight With John Oliver —which once cautioned viewers against voting for Trump by reminding them of his family’s historical surname, Drumpf—is still going too, and in a recent episode covered Trump’s efforts to reshape the Department of Justice. Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers have consistently pursued Trump since his rise; even Jimmy Fallon, who was once reluctant to get political , will now occasionally take a shot. Some new impersonators have risen to take Baldwin’s place: James Austin Johnson and Shane Gillis have both played the president with some success in recent years. But in this cohort, things aren’t quite the same as they were. Johnson’s impression hasn’t created the kind of splash that Baldwin’s once did; his version of Trump is reminiscent of the de rigueur presidential impressions of SNL seasons past. (That’s no judgment of comedic value—Johnson’s version is as accurate as it gets.) And last year, when CBS decided to end its long-running program The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , late-night TV lost one of its most prominent and consistent critics. The administration’s attempts to chill dissenting speech elsewhere, although disturbing, don’t appear to have suppressed this sort of comedy’s prevalence in American culture. And in one case, such attempts had the opposite effect: In September, ABC suspended Kimmel’s show after Federal Communications Committee Chairman Brendan Carr demanded that it do so; a few days later, in response to a public outcry, the network reversed course. The fracas turned out to be good for ratings—Kimmel’s first show back was its most-watched in more than a decade. [ Read: Jimmy Kimmel ran right at his critics ] Still, the old guard doesn’t totally see the point. “All the majors that continue to just throttle him and carry on about him—move on to other people!” Baldwin told me. “It’s not gonna make any difference.” Atamanuik told me that by fixating on Trump, comedians risk missing the bigger issues, and that young people especially have “an anger at the entire system.” (The top-three late-night talk shows have been fighting for viewers in the coveted 18–49 age demographic for more than a decade.) “They know that Trump is just a product of something else,” he said. Meanwhile, Cooper said a few years ago that she has “no desire” to revisit her lip-syncs, and that “there’s nothing left to really do with it.” Brent Terhune, another veteran of the short-form-video scene that flourished during the coronavirus pandemic, is less gloomy about the future of Trump-inflected comedy. This is partially because he’s not interested in taking on the president directly. Instead, he makes videos in the persona of a Trump fan. The character he’s played for nearly a decade, “Alpha Male,” is a sort of disgruntled MAGA vlogger—“a reaction and a reflection of people that are Trump die-hards,” Terhune told me. Part of what distinguishes the performance is that it’s at least somewhat empathetic; he said he’s always being told that Alpha Male reminds people of their brothers, dads, and uncles. His view is that because the Alpha Male character isn’t just about skewering Trump, it could potentially outlast his administration. Terhune’s enthusiasm has certainly outlasted that of many of his peers, so maybe on-screen political comedy is just in need of new subjects. Although Atamanuik no longer consistently plays Trump, he has lately been impersonating Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—and Baldwin suggested that House Speaker Mike Johnson and former Acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte could be deserving targets. Or maybe you can make the same joke only so many times before you start wondering what it is you’re really doing. In 1962, when the impressionist Vaughn Meader released his landmark comedy album, The First Family , which poked fun at the Kennedys, the anthropologist Margaret Mead remarked that its very existence illuminated something about American society. “This making fun of people in authority is very healthy,” she told Life magazine . “It is the difference between democracy and tyranny.” The impressionists I spoke with might hesitate to agree with that assessment. But beyond the easy laugh of a presidential impersonation, humor can still be a potent force in defending a free society against tyranny—that is, if comedians are willing to keep finding new angles rather than repeat old gags.

items.title: The Gun Lobby’s Most Cynical Move Yet
items.description: As a newspaper reporter, I covered my first school shooting in 2007 at Virginia Tech, where 32 students and faculty were murdered and 17 others were wounded. In one story , I recounted how Emily, a 19-year-old sophomore, was lying partially behind a desk on the floor of her French class while the shooter gunned down her teacher and nearly every student around her before shooting himself in the head. I can’t forget the image of Emily, shot twice herself, who pretended to be dead but surreptitiously grabbed a cellphone on the floor that another student had used to call 911 before he was shot. I listened many weeks later to a recording of the call. At first, she was too terrified to speak. All the police dispatcher could hear was the sound of her breath and the loud pop pop pop of gunfire all around her. “I can’t talk,” she whispered, gasping for breath. “Please hurry.” After the Virginia Tech massacre, I reported on many other school shootings, including Sandy Hook in 2012, when twenty 6- and 7-year-olds were shot to death in their first-grade classrooms and six staff members were killed. Attorney General Eric Holder, whom I covered at the time as The Washington Post ’s Justice Department reporter, told me that walking through the bullet-riddled classrooms still caked with blood was the most difficult day of his professional life. He later cried openly when he saw the crime-scene photos of the children lying dead in their classrooms. I wrote about so many school massacres that I lost count. After each one, I reached out to the National Rifle Association, the National Shooting Sports Foundation (the gun industry’s trade association), and other organizations that the nation’s gun lobby comprises for their response. They rarely commented beyond a statement offering thoughts and prayers to the victims and their families. I twice attended the world’s largest firearms trade show, held annually in Las Vegas for tens of thousands of gun makers, sellers, and other professionals but closed to the general public. There, too, leaders of the NRA, other advocates, and representatives of the multibillion-dollar gun industry would not comment on school shootings, except to reiterate their support for armed guards in schools and a government registry of mentally ill people, and to resist calls to strengthen background checks and restrict access to semi-automatic rifles such as the AR-15. [ William H. Frist: The politics of gun safety are changing. I should know. ] But the gun lobby had another response to school shootings behind the scenes—one I didn’t know about at the time. A study by Stanford University researchers this year found that after fatal school shootings, pro-gun political-action committees dramatically increased their contributions to their preferred U.S. House candidates in the districts where the shootings occurred, when those races were competitive. These shifts in spending were not observed after other incidents of mass gun violence or after nonfatal school shootings—only when children were killed in schools. Over the many years that I reported on gun violence, the gun lobby’s enormous campaign spending was no secret. But the Stanford study reveals how these groups targeted their money, raising their aggressive tactics to a new level. In the first study of its kind, the authors analyzed 25 years of data, linking campaign-finance records to every fatal K–12 school shooting from 2000 to 2024. They then compared campaign contributions between the districts that did and did not have a school shooting. After school shootings where children died, pro-gun contributions to candidates in competitive congressional districts increased on average by more than 30 percent. And when the shooting occurred within two months of an election, contributions surged by 2,820 percent. “The data shows that the gun lobby saves its political firepower for the moments when public grief is greatest and lawmakers are under the most pressure to act,” Eric A. Baldwin, one of the authors, told me. In November 2021, for example, a 15-year-old killed four students and injured seven other people at Oxford High School, in Michigan. The pro-gun PACs contributed $50,650 during the 2021–22 election cycle in the district where the high school was located, a 434 percent increase from the previous cycle and a 591 percent increase from an average of the previous five cycles, according to the Stanford researchers. In December 2013, a 17-year-old senior was killed at Arapahoe High School, in a suburb of Denver. Before the shooting, the pro-gun PAC contribution had been $1,000. Afterward, it soared to $49,470. Gun-safety PACs also increased their spending in competitive districts after school shootings. But the pro-gun groups were by far the dominant spenders until 2018, the year of the Parkland shooting, which left 17 students and faculty dead at a high school in Florida; at that point, gun-safety groups began to significantly increase their spending, sometimes equaling or even surpassing the spending of the pro-gun groups. The Stanford researchers did not find that increased spending by either side after fatal school shootings measurably affected which party actually won a competitive House election. (The districts that the study looked at represent only a subset of the gun lobby’s overall election spending.) Nevertheless, the study shows how pro-gun PACs work to undermine anti-gun feelings in communities suffering from the trauma of children being killed in schools. In poll after poll for more than a decade, the majority of Americans have favored stricter gun laws. Most Americans specifically want a ban on weapons such as AR-15s , and also favor stricter background checks. That sentiment is particularly acute after a school shooting, when “public demand for reform is especially high,” according to the Stanford researchers. But, they write, the pro-gun spending surge means that “instead of yielding to constituent pressure, candidates are fortified to resist it and are empowered to reframe their opposition to reform as principled rather than unresponsive.” [ Tyler Austin Harper: ‘How much blood is your fun worth?’ ] Although the NRA’s power has been waning in recent years, it still spent $10 million in the 2024 election. Other pro-gun groups have emerged and are influencing national policy; together with the NRA, they spend about $14 million a year on lobbying. In response to lawsuits from a number of pro-gun entities, including Gun Owners of America, a federal judge in Texas recently found unconstitutional a 1934 federal law that placed strict requirements on anyone purchasing silencers, short-barreled rifles, and shotguns, among other firearms. The Justice Department did not immediately appeal the ruling. In recent months, the Trump administration has announced new actions to make it easier for gun purchasers to avoid background checks when obtaining firearms. In April, then–Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Justice Department officials announced the rollback of gun regulations alongside leaders from the NRA, the National Shooting Sports Foundation, the National Association for Guns Rights, and Gun Owners of America. And House Republicans proposed a bill to cut nearly $300 million from the budget of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the agency that enforces the nation’s gun laws. The killing of America’s children and teenagers in their classrooms has become normalized. From a young age, our children and grandchildren are being taught vocabulary and math alongside lessons in how to hide when an “active shooter” storms their classrooms. The Stanford study is a compelling reminder of how far the gun lobby will go to block any efforts to protect our children.

items.title: What It Takes to Reclaim Your Attention Span
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Pocket Casts Of all the potential effects of using smartphones, the one that seems to inspire the most anxiety is what scrolling could be doing to people’s attention. On social media (ironically), many people express a desire to “heal” their attention spans from the damage they feel technology has done. They’re picking up on something real. In one 2025 study , researchers found that blocking the internet on people’s phones for two weeks led to improvements in sustained attention equivalent to reversing 10 years of cognitive decline. In this final episode of How to Touch Grass , host Julie Beck embarks on an experiment to see if she can heal her own attention span. Beck and co-host Natalie Brennan also hear from Jenny Odell, the author of How to Do Nothing and Saving Time , about how Odell’s antagonism for her phone actually helped her make peace with it, and how nature can teach us to pay deeper attention to the world around us. The following is a transcript of the episode: [ Music ] Julie Beck: Are you happy with your relationship with your phone, or are you not happy with it? Person 1: I wish I could reduce some of the Instagram Reel-ing, particularly at night, where I kind of go down the rabbit hole and it’s like, Oh my God, it’s midnight. Beck: Oh, yeah. I’ve been there. It’s like lost time. You know like when the aliens come and they get you, and then they put you back down, and it’s just lost time. Person 2: It has impacted my attention span. I get bored after half a paragraph of reading. Beck: Do you have a sense in your mind of when you noticed that you feel like your attention span was getting worse? Person 2: Probably been, like, since the start of COVID, probably in the last five years. Person 3: The thing that kills me sometimes is how much I want to look stuff up in conversations. I still constantly have a few books that I’m trying to read through and trying to rebuild attention, or something like that. Beck: I’m Julie Beck, a staff writer at The Atlantic . Natalie Brennan: And I’m Natalie Brennan, a producer at The Atlantic . Beck: This is How to Touch Grass . [ Birds chirping ] Brennan: Julie, attention is one of the biggest things we’ve heard people talk about when they are renegotiating their relationship to their phone. Beck: Ironically, I feel like every time I go on social media these days, I see someone talking about how they’re trying to heal their attention span from technology that they’re currently using. Brennan: ( Laughs .) Yes. Beck: And it’s always that word too, heal . It’s like we’re sick or we’re injured, and we must heal. Brennan: Is it something that you’ve been worried about? Beck: I do worry about my attention sometimes. Like every time I go to the gym lately, I forget to lock the locker that they have in the locker room. I put my stuff in there; I shut the door. Brennan: And you don’t lock? Beck: Then I guess I simply walk away. Brennan: Huh! Beck : And I don’t realize until I get back that—I mean, no one has taken my stuff, luckily, so it’s all good. Good Samaritans out there. But that has happened not once, not twice, more than twice. ( Laughs. ) Brennan: I guess the way that the attention-span thing comes up for me the most is when I think about the number of hours that I spend on my phone. Beck: You’re pouring your attention into that phone. Brennan: Yeah, I see those as very interconnected. But I’ve also noticed that I very actively try not to think about it. I rush to swipe away the screen-time notification every Sunday. Obviously, that anxiety points to the fact that I want to have a different relationship with my phone, right? Beck: What do you think has stopped you from actively trying to get that screen time down? Brennan: I think it’s scary to sit with ourselves when we have grown really accustomed to all the stimuli. Beck: Mmm. Love stimuli. [ Music ] Jenny Odell: We talk a lot about, you know, looking at your phone as a negative thing, and we talk about it in the negative, right? Like, I wanna do less of this thing. There’s this thing that I do a lot; I wanna do less of it . And there’s not as much talk about what I wanna do more of . Beck: That’s Jenny Odell, the author of How to Do Nothing . When that book came out in 2019, and I remember at the time it was one of the first things I read that really raised a concern about what modern technology and social media were doing specifically to people’s attention. So now it’s seven years later, and I asked Jenny how her thinking has evolved and how she’s doing with her own screen-time habits. Odell: I mean, I’m … [( Laughs. )] Look, I’m doing great. Beck: That’s—I’m so happy to hear it. I can’t say the same. ( Laughs. ) Odell: I’m okay with my relationship with my phone and screen time. Beck: So can you walk me through a little bit? Odell: Yeah. I would say, like, part of the attention economy is the selling of quick fixes when, you know, habits form over time. They’re like grooves, right? Like, they need to be sort of formed over time. And so … Beck: Like, geologically. Odell: Yes, exactly. And I think, you know, if you try to, say, go cold turkey, it can be frustrating when you don’t see immediate results. Beck: Yeah. Odell: Or even within a couple of months, right? And then in that meantime, there’s all this uphill struggle of, like, your friends are still doing it. You need to be on Instagram to see this and that, and there’s just muscle-memory things, things you’re used to. You get up in the morning; you look at your phone. These are just—that’s hard. Like, those things are really ingrained, especially, I think, if you’re younger. I’m good now. But I just wanna stress that it took some time, and in that time there’s a little bit of a leap of faith. Beck: Yeah. I mean, I deleted TikTok off my phone for the third or fourth time, who’s counting? But like you were saying, the muscle memory of, like, the thumb going up and down, has just transferred to Instagram unfortunately. So we gotta work on that. Odell: I would say there’s, honestly, you know, I’m almost 40. Actually standing, like, with your very heavy head, like on your neck; when you get older, you start to notice the problems from that, and it’s like that is another kind of physical limit. I can’t sit at a computer for that long without injuring myself. And then I think I really had to think about my relationship to the news was a really big one that I hadn’t quite figured out. When you’re kind of scrolling, you're scrolling through it, you’re not really deeply engaging with any one particular issue. Beck: Yeah. Odell: You’re just seeing a list of bad things, and they’re bad in all different kinds of ways, and they’re terrible. Like, even just sitting with one of those things produces this paralysis. It’s like, in order to do something, you need an orientation toward the future and a situation in which you feel that you have some agency. There are certain things that I have started to do in the last couple years. One of them is volunteering at a native-plant-restoration project every week. I’ve also been going to a lot of repair fairs. Also kind of volunteering-type things that are in person. Beck: Where you bring like a broken toaster or something— Odell: Yeah.. Beck: —and learn how to fix it. Odell : And learn how to fix it. Yeah. Totally. When I’m there, there is no desire to look at my phone. Like, it’s just so far from my mind, and it has this weird lasting effect throughout the week, actually, because I had this experience that was so direct, that was so meaningful. Beck: And tell me what is the good thing about the repair café, about the, you know, weeding the native plants? Like, what is the good thing? Odell: I think, you know, some of it is just recognition. I think we as humans, we want to be socially recognized, right? We want to feel seen. We wanna feel heard. We wanna feel welcomed. You know, it’s like Cheers or whatever. Beck: ( Laughs. ) Odell: Like, you wanna walk into a room and have people be like, Hey, it’s you. I know you.I’m happy to see you . This is just kind of like a really basic thing that we want. I kinda think that social media, especially early on, the evil genius of it was that it was hijacking that. And so I feel like these are in-person events. I feel incredibly recognized and acknowledged. And then it’s like, when you feel This is the real thing , it becomes very obvious what is not the real thing. That’s a big part of it. And I think you’re there. You have a shared project. You’re getting some traction with something, right? Instead of just sort of constantly being washed over with information and not really having anything to grasp onto. Beck: For most people in this day and age, totally going without a smartphone just isn’t possible, or at least not practical. Like, the infrastructure of society, you know, they’ve got the QR-code menu at the restaurant, the stores are all accepting Apple Pay and Google Pay, and so many websites require you to receive a text and then put the code in to even get in there. So trying to resist getting sucked into your phone just feels like resisting the inevitable sometimes. Have you found a way to resolve this tension for yourself? Odell: I live in the same society you’re describing, and I just used my phone to pay for lunch before this. But then I put it away. Beck: Mmm. Odell: I use the phrase standing apart as a way of kind of not leaving or believing in the fantasy of escape from something, and just sort of being like, I’m standing in a position from which I can see the thing. Beck: You’re not running away from it or— Odell: But I have critical distance. And I think about something like food. You know, you go to the grocery store and, I mean, depending on the grocery store you’re in, you kind of understand that 80 percent of the food in it is bad for you. We kinda know that, right? It has been that way long enough. Beck: Doesn’t stop me from getting the Flamin’ Hot Cheetos, but yes. I do know. Odell: ( Laughs. ) But it’s just this understanding that that space is just not set up for me to thrive. Beck: Mm. Odell: And I think that it’s helpful to maybe transpose that to your phone. What is a phone? A phone is a communication device. What I want from this is communication. The apps, you know, social media in particular, are not designed for you to thrive. They are designed for the opposite. ( Laughs. ) These are actively bad for me, and I won’t feel good. For me, it’s sort of a level of acceptance of, like, antagonism has been helpful. Where it’s like, I’m never going to have a peaceful relationship with that universe, and I’m just gonna kind of accept that and take what I need and leave. Beck: You know, recently I hear so many people, both online and in real life, talking about, “healing their attention spans” from the damage that they feel like technology has done. And I’m curious why, of all the things, you think people are worried about their attention specifically. Odell: One would hope that what you pay attention to is what is important to you. That’s an ideal situation. Beck: Not always the case. Odell: Right, exactly. So if you’re not paying attention to things that are important to you, there’s something, I think, like, deeply unsettling about that on the level of identity because it’s like, Am I even who I am? Right? Am I who I want to be if I’m paying my attention to something that I don’t feel I ever chose? Beck: Yeah. Odell: I think it really deeply affects people on the level of, like, self-control and their sort of understanding of their identity. Beck: Yeah. Well, it seems like the solution that many people have landed on for healing their attention span is just trying to be online less, however they can. So do you think that logging off is the answer, or no? Odell: I think that the best approach, personally, is to just treat it as an experiment. Honestly, it makes it interesting, like I’m a curious person and I’m curious about myself and my own reaction to things. Kind of being like, Okay, I’m gonna try this. I’m gonna see what happens when I try this. [ Music ] Beck: Natalie, immediately after this interview, I really felt the itch to do what Jenny said—to try an experiment. And when I was thinking about how to do that, I remembered this study I had seen from 2025 where researchers blocked the internet on people’s smartphones for two weeks. Brennan: Okay. Beck: And just doing that, they found that the improvement to people’' sustained attention was equivalent to reversing 10 years of cognitive decline. Brennan: After two weeks? Beck: After two weeks. Brennan: That discrepancy feels huge. Beck: It’s huge. So I tried the experiment on myself for two weeks. Now, I didn’t perfectly replicate the conditions of the 2025 study, to be clear. They blocked mobile internet using an app called Freedom. I used, instead, this device called a Brick. Brennan: Huge among my friends. Beck: Oh, your friends are all into it. Brennan: Yes. Beck: Okay, so you know. So I used this device. I picked all the apps I was gonna block, and you have to physically touch your phone to the device to unlock it. Brennan: Right. Beck: I tried to, you know, keep all of the things that would allow me to communicate with other people, and so I blocked all games; I blocked all social media, email, Slack, internet browsers, and most internet-connected apps. Brennan: Okay. Beck: So I blocked all of that for 23 hours a day. I was allowed one hour of non-Bricked time if I needed or wanted it. And I could do whatever I wanted on a computer, same as in the study. It was only the phone that was restricted. Brennan: And how were you going to test this? Beck: So I got in touch with someone from that 2025 study, and they shared an attention pre-test with me and a self-report questionnaire. So I took those for a baseline. Brennan: How long was the test? Beck: It felt like 1,000 hours. Brennan: Totally. ( Laughs. ) Beck: I think he told me it’s actually, like, eight minutes. ( Laughs. ) I did both of those things before I started the experiment, and then I took them again at the end of the experiment. And I agreed to record a little audio diary along the way. [ Music ] Beck: Captain’s log, day one. My phone has been Bricked pretty much all day. I’ve definitely been kinda low energy. I don’t know if that’s, like, dopamine withdrawal. I’ve definitely been carrying my phone around with me everywhere even though there’s not really that much for me to look at. Morning, it’s day two. My husband is out of town right now, so it is daunting to have two of my biggest sources of entertainment, my husband and my phone, unavailable to me at this time, but we persevere. It is Saturday. It’s my first full weekend day. I ordered a big order of yarn, so I have a lot of knitting and crochet stuff to work on. Good morning, it’s day five. Knitting right now. Joe and I went birding. The one thing that I am noticing mood-wise is that I do feel pretty calm, like maybe more calm than usual. Brennan: OK, Julie! First check-in. What off the bat did you think you were going to do more of with your time that you didn’t wind up doing? Beck: Using the phone as a phone, as a communication device. Actually, like, calling my loved ones to catch up, you know, what the phone was invented for. Shout-out Alexander Graham Bell. But I think because I had blocked so much, and I was getting more used to just not having my phone on me and in my hand at all times, I was just thinking about my phone less overall, which was the goal.But I kinda come to think that as much as the distraction of the phone, like, has a cost, there’s also a cost to putting more distance there, because the phone is where the people are. Brennan: It’s interesting how much our relationship to our phones is intertwined with our relationship to others. Beck: Yeah. Brennan: When we overuse our phones, that isn’t good for our relationships, and the way we use our phones is definitely influenced by other people. [ Music ] Odell: I think we don’t realize how much of our habits kind of live in other people. Like, think about it. When do you pick up your phone? It’s when the person you’re talking to picks up their phone, right? Like, the person picks up their phone; what are you gonna do? Sit there? Stare into space? That habit, like, lives between people. Beck: It’s so true, because my friends will, you know, text me TikToks still even though I am trying to get off TikTok. And then if I’m like, Okay, I’ll just watch the, like, Lord of the Rings meme that they sent me , of course my phone prompts me like, Don’t you wanna download TikTok again? And so it is, like, sort of driven by, like, the relationship of wanting to see this meme. But I guess my bigger question is: Is logging off to pay attention to something else in the real world actually better, or is it just different? Odell: I always think about, like, if you saw someone hiking and looking at their phone, you could be like, That’s so depressing. But then it’s like, what if they’re looking at iNaturalist? Beck: Yeah. Odell: And they’re, like, identifying a plant. There are good things on the phone; there are bad things on the phone. There are good things IRL; there are bad things IRL. One thing that you can say is that the sort of quality of attention that one often experiences on the phone with things like social media is pretty narrow versus things off the phone. There are so many different kinds of experience, so many different scales of time, so many different scales of space. I love seeing movies in a movie theater. Beck: Oh, yeah. Me too. Odell: I’m like a movie-theater junkie. I love to see horror movies in a theater. Beck: Oh. Not me. Odell: So there’s things like that, but then there’s things like looking at a very small bird in your neighborhood, or being at a table with a group of people and being part of a conversation. Like, these are all just so different. Even if you think about your body in those spaces; it’s so different. I think it’s good to have a variety of different contexts for your attention.I think that’s probably healthy. [ Music ] Beck: We’re gonna take a quick break but when we come back: how the way we think about our phones affects the ways we use them. Odell: I think about it more as like: When I look at it as an object, it looks like a tool. And it did not look like a tool to me before. It looked like a black hole. Beck: Like a portal to the underworld or something. Brennan: Plus, did Julie fix her attention span? The results of her experiment, coming up. [ Break ] Beck: So day six, and wouldn’t you freaking know it, I did the exact same thing at the gym again. Sure enough, I forgot to lock it again . I’m legitimately concerned. Anyway, my attention is not fixed yet! Good morning. It’s day seven of the experiment. My average screen time is down 74 percent from last week. I certainly haven’t been, like a perfect screen-abstinent person this week. I’ve watched plenty of TV. I have been able to, I think, focus a bit better. I read 200 pages of my book yesterday. I wonder how much of this could be achieved without such a draconian approach. I’ve been pretty surprised by how quickly I kind of, like, submitted. But yeah, just how quickly the cravings to check my phone all the time really receded. Brennan: Julie, day 7 was midway through your experiment. What started to shift for you by that point? Did the way you think about your phone start to change? Beck: I think what you learn, or at least what I learned when you block access to almost everything on your phone, is that the phone is not just one thing. There’s a lot of different stuff in there. Like— Brennan: Yeah. Beck: —you know? I think in our frustration with our attention span sometimes, people, myself included, will demonize the phone as a device. Like, smartphones are evil. Smartphones are sucking our life force, and they’re making us stupid, and that kind of flattens the problem, I think. What kept coming up for me is there’s a lot of different things I turn to my phone for, and some of them are more problematic than others. Like, checking the weather is, uh, very helpful. Brennan: You made a mistake in blocking that one ( Laughs. ) Beck: I did. Like, I realized that actually the first day. But I suppose that is the point of the experiment, right? To figure out which parts of my phone are actually adding to my life and which are taking away from it. [ Music ] Beck: Jenny, have you heard of these devices that block certain apps on your phone? There’s the Freedom app, the Unplug, the Brick device. Odell: Yeah. Beck : What do you think of the recent popularity of these things? Odell: Honestly, I’m all for it. I don’t use any—I’m not trying to brag. I don’t need them. I think they’re great. There’s one in particular that I think is called SocialFocus, and it lets you kind of change the appearance of websites. Like, you could go to YouTube and not see the auto suggestions, for example. Beck: Mmm. Odell: Or maybe not see comments. It kind of allows you to change what you see. And I think there was a Chrome extension that came out called News Feed Eradicator. And guess what happened? I stopped going to Facebook. And I didn’t decide to do that. It was because the News Feed is there to keep you on Facebook. So if you eradicate it, replace it with some sort of mindfulness quote, you go to the site; it’s inert. It can’t grab you in that way. Beck: Hmm. Odell: And so I just simply stopped going. It was a totally unremarkable thing. I didn’t even tell anyone, Oh, I’m quitting Facebook. I just stopped going to it. And I think that’s really powerful. So that’s why I’m a big fan of anything that can give someone sort of granular control over what the—it sort of reintroduced choice in areas where people have never experienced choice. Because that, in and of itself, will cause someone to reflect upon what it is that they want. Beck: All of this reminds me of a study I’ve been thinking of a lot lately, that found using an app that was similar to the Brick for two weeks had such a big effect on people’s attention spans that it amounted to, like, reversing 10 years of cognitive decline— Beck: Oh my God. Beck: —which seems really huge. Odell: Wow. That’s incredible. I’m surprised and not surprised. Actually, honestly, this reminds me of, like, ecological restoration because when you restore a site, some things come back quickly and some things don’t, right? Like, you restore a wetland, some species are gonna come back almost immediately. The nutrient cycling of the entire site might take 100 years. Maybe our attention is similar in that, or our behavior, let’s say, it takes a long time to totally overhaul something. But at the same time, I think you might be surprised at how quickly certain things change. Like, in times when I was a little bit more embroiled online and using my phone a lot, and then I would maybe go somewhere, put it away for a while or whatever, I found that after a couple of days, I would notice that my attention felt different. Beck: Hmm. Odell: And by attention felt different, I mean I would notice details or small differences in things. It’s almost like having a higher-resolution image or something. Beck: Are there other seemingly small changes to your routine that you feel like might have that kind of big cognitive benefit? Odell: You know, I think trying to replace habits with other habits—I meditate in the morning, only just for, like, 10 minutes. I kind of calm down to a level where then it’s not going to as easily occur to me to then pick up my phone, or at least I'll be a little bit more reflective about it. Beck: Yeah. My thing so far, my recent thing has been taking up knitting and crochet, and this seems so small, but it’s like now while I’m watching TV, instead of looking at my phone, my hands are in hand jail, right? Doing knitting. Odell: ( Laughs. ) Hand jail. Beck: And it doesn’t seem so virtuous when I’m like, Now I’m only looking at one screen , but I feel like, you know, it’s an improvement. Odell: I think that’s great. Beck: Maybe I'll get down to zero screens, TBD. But the other layer to that that I was just thinking about when it comes to phones and social media and stuff is, like, a lot of times where I’m going to learn how to do this new stitch or whatever is YouTube. Odell: Mm-hmm. Beck: So it’s not, you know, one is totally replacing the other, but there is sort of a relationship. Like now I am using that tool kind of for this other thing. Odell: Yeah. Right, and I think that points to an important distinction, which is maybe a bit more nuanced than just, say, screen time as a statistic. You know, you were asking earlier about my changed relationship to my phone. Beck: Mm-hmm. Odell: I think about it more as like: When I look at it as an object, it looks like a tool. And it did not look like a tool to me before. It looked like a black hole. Beck: Like a portal to the underworld or something. Odell: Yeah. Or, frankly, I wasn’t even looking at it. I’m already picking it up. Like, I’m already in there. I’m already in that world. There wasn’t even a point where I perceived the phone as an object. Beck: Yeah. You skipped right ahead. Odell: Yeah. And now I feel like the things that I use it for: the Merlin app, it’s like Shazam for bird songs, I use that. I use iNaturalist. I use the Constellation app, voice memos for, you know, recording birds. That relationship, to me, feels really different because the intention and the purpose, I feel like I’m in control of that. I mean on my phone, the first home screen is all what I would call observational apps, so camera, voice memo, iNaturalist, Merlin. Beck: Mm. Odell: I’m kind of trying to remind myself of how I wanna use the phone. Like, I now associate my phone with those activities. Beck: You write a lot about nature. Odell: Yeah. Beck: Being inspired by nature, how being in nature helps you, you know, pay attention. A common piece of advice for those who have been brain-rotted by the internet is to go touch grass. So are you also telling us to touch grass? Odell: Yeah, pretty much. And, I mean, the weeds that I weed at my weekly project are grass, so— Beck: And you’re touching them. Odell: —actually, I’m saying Kill grass . No, I’m just kidding. ( Laughs. ) But the reason I think it became such a—that phrase caught on was because it’s just so obviously true. The obvious truth of it is, like, why it’s funny and annoying at the same time. Beck: Yeah. What is it that you think the natural world has to teach us about attention? Odell: Complexity, basically. Like, I think it's a master class in complexity. It is kind of an antidote to the idea of the easy answer, which I think—I really blame Instagram for the oversimplification of political issues.Like, personally, that is just my ax to grind. And the idea that you could sort of absolve yourself by reposting something is just—yeah. It’s upsetting to me. But I think that there’s no easy answers to anything. Like, if you are a birder and you like birds, well, guess what? You’re gonna have to learn about trees. Beck: Mm-hmm. Odell: And then gonna have to learn about, like, seasons, and then, I don’t know, there’s just—everything is so tied to everything else, and there are so many things that are sort of, like, neither good nor bad or sort of arguable. We need lessons in that right now. Like, we need lessons in the sort of, like, Let me pick a point in space to look at, and then let me look at the context around that. Okay, now let me look at the context around that. And now you’ve sort of widened this whole ecosystem. I think the opposite of that is what happens online. Beck: So Jenny, if someone is just starting to rethink the relationship they have with their devices, what advice would you give them? Odell: Try to take an outsider’s perspective on yourself. I’m a big journaler, so I’ve journaled since I was a kid. So that would work for me. I would look at my phone, I would look at some stuff on my phone, and then I would just write down, kinda what it was and then how I felt about it. And I would be, like, brutally honest. Beck: Oh, man. Odell: Just pretend like you’re a scientist. And just talk to a friend about it. You could write it down, like, whatever. But, you know, I think there needs to be that, like, every so often you step to the side and you go, Okay, what did I just do? Like, Why did I do that? How did that make me feel? You can be super brief about it. Just do it for a week. Just see what it tells you. Beck: Yeah. Odell: Before you try to make any changes, because the danger is that a person feels shame, they feel that it’s bad. They’re like, Okay, I need to change this , and then they try really hard to change it, and then it doesn’t go the way they wanted, and then they feel more shame. And now it’s just, like, a spiral.
