[ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The right is changing the rules of the culture war ] There was the Great Pierogi Incident last year at the West Tisbury farmers’ market, in which a vendor refused to sell half a dozen dumplings to Dershowitz, citing his representation of “several sexual predators and abusers, including Jeffrey Epstein.” Dershowitz claimed that he was being discriminated against over his vocal support for Israel and initiated a follow-up spectacle a week later in which the vendor, Krem Miskevich, refused to accept a signed copy of one of Dershowitz’s books ( The Ten Big Anti-Israel Lies ) as a peace offering. In 2022, Dershowitz said he’d received a fan email from a reader who alleged that he’d been beaten up at the beach (he did not specify where) just for carrying a copy of a book written by Dershowitz. “Without warning, I was slugged and punched in the face,” the man wrote to Dershowitz, who reprinted the unverified email on Substack in a post titled “Email From a Man Who Got Beaten Up for Reading My Book.” And then there was the infamous clash at the Chilmark General Store with Dershowitz’s now very-much-ex-friend Larry David. In the annals of Dershowitz’s social spiral on the Vineyard, this conflagration has taken on almost-mythic dimensions, like his own personal Stalingrad. Dershowitz was sitting on the porch of the store with another friend, “who happened to be a very kind of radical woke lefty from New York, but very tolerant,” he told me. David was not very tolerant, at least of Dershowitz. He walked onto the porch, refused to shake Dershowitz’s hand, called him “disgusting,” and stormed off. Dershowitz said at the time that David was so irate, Dershowitz worried that the comedian might suffer a stroke. That unpleasantness on the porch, memorialized on Page Six , took place five summers ago. But Dershowitz talks about it as if it were yesterday. On a recent Saturday, I ventured north from Washington for a little hardship duty in Chilmark, the preciously pastoral town on the western side of the island where Dershowitz has owned a home since 1991. I approached him first by email, telling Dershowitz that I was curious about his current social standing on the Vineyard and how things were going for him this summer. The subject matter could be freshly topical, I figured, because his two most prominent clients—Trump and Epstein—are more toxic than ever. To my surprise, Dershowitz agreed to speak with me. Actually, I was not surprised. “W e can meet on the porch for a slice,” he proposed. Dershowitz, who turns 88 next month, has been presiding from the rocking chairs of the Chilmark General Store for decades, juggling pizza and discourse. When I arrived, I found him wearing a bright-red T-shirt with the words Proud American over an Israeli flag and an American one, each in the shape of a heart. He told me that he’d asked his wife, Carolyn Cohen, to join us but she had no interest. “She said, ‘I’m so sick and tired of this subject,’” he told me. Dershowitz conceded that he, too, is weary of it. “But, you know, it’s important that people get the whole context,” he said. The whole context, in 2026, is basically this: Dershowitz says he has started a new life on the Vineyard. But just because his persecution tale has become an island eye-roll does not mean that it has subsided. Especially, according to Dershowitz, in his own, bucolic neighborhood. “Here in Chilmark, it’s 90 percent negative,” Dershowitz reported to me. That reception contrasts with what he gets in Miami Beach, where he spends his winters and where, he said, he is treated “wonderfully.” He is “treated very well” even in the more heavily trafficked Vineyard towns on the other side of the island. “In Edgartown and even Oak Bluffs, the African American community, I’m treated very well,” he said. “It’s all Chilmark. And it’s all Jewish, anti-Zionist.” I noted that he can at least still hold court at the Chilmark General Store. But he argued with my choice of the term holding court . “I used to—not anymore,” he said. “You don’t hold court anymore?” I asked, as he arguably held court. “What is this?” “You’re interviewing me,” he said. In the past, it would have been a high-end conclave. “Normally, we would have this whole area,” he said, motioning to a group of rocking chairs on one side of the porch. “I would have Larry David here,” he said. “Ted Danson was here sometimes,” he added. “The guy who did Ghostbusters —he died a few years ago—he was here.” (This was Harold Ramis, who died in 2014.) “The whole crew of Chilmark friends, I would say, 20 or so, no longer talk to me,” Dershowitz said. He pointed next door to the Chilmark Tavern, one of his favorite restaurants on the Vineyard, where he claims that some of his vacation nemeses are trying to get him banned. “A bunch of people went to the Chilmark Tavern and said If you continue to serve Dershowitz, we’re not coming here ,” he insisted. I was skeptical of this. “Ask her; you can check with her,” he said. “Jenny.” When I contacted Jenna Petersiel, the proprietor of the Chilmark Tavern, she told me that she’d assumed that The Atlantic wanted to speak with her about the challenges of running a restaurant, or ticks. “A discussion of Alan Dershowitz had not crossed my mind,” she said, declining to comment otherwise. Dershowitz also told me of an event he had attended on the Chilmark Tavern deck not long ago. A woman got out of her car, he claimed, “saw I was up there, turned around, and went back to her car.” He appears to have a limitless supply of such stories, in part because it seems as if Dershowitz initiates a fair number of confrontations himself. The week before our conversation, he had returned to the hallowed cultural battleground of the Pierogi Wars, the West Tisbury farmers’ market. He was wearing his U.S.-Israel shirt (or “my Zionist T-shirt,” of which he has two—one red, one blue) and saw a guy wearing a Free Palestine shirt. “I walked up to him. I said, ‘Can we take a picture together?’” The man refused. “He said, ‘No, no, no Israel,’ and he walked away.” Dershowitz believes that many of his old Vineyard friends revile him for calling out the “anti-Zionist” and “radical” bent of the progressive left. He showed me his phone and cued up what he calls “my daily love note.” This one was an unsolicited email he’d just received, with “GENOCIDAL ZIONIST ISRAEL!” in the subject line; he kindly forwarded the note to me. “They always combine Zionism with pedophilia,” Dershowitz observed of his correspondents. A few times during our conversation, I questioned Dershowitz about whether people really reject him because of his Zionist views or whether it might involve something more comprehensive: him being Alan Dershowitz. His position on the Middle East seems farther down the list of reasons that people might not like him than his affiliations with Trump and Epstein and his overall reputation, accrued over decades. But Dershowitz claims, for instance, that he’s no longer asked to speak at the Martha’s Vineyard Book Festival because “they censor anybody they disagree with.” (A spokesperson for the book festival told me in an email that Dershowitz’s claim is “completely false” and that “the festival line up over the past two decades hardly reflects a narrow or excluding agenda.”) “I personify what the woke hates,” Dershowitz said. Before I could ask him what, exactly, “the woke” is, he explained that he is now seen as a “traitor” to the Democratic Party. The enmity is mutual. In September, he has a new book coming out called Why I Quit the Dems: And So Should You! The subtitle is Confessions of a Reluctant Republican . I asked Dershowitz directly whether he had voted for Trump in 2024. “You’re allowed to ask it,” he said. “And my wife does not allow me to answer it.” “Okay, so you’re going to hide behind your wife,” I said. “I’m going to hide behind my wife,” he confirmed. For the record, Dershowitz added that he always votes, and said that he had not voted for Kamala Harris. Also, his new book includes a blurb from President Trump (who obviously read every word). Alan Dershowitz watches as Donald Trump speaks to the media at Manhattan Criminal Court in May 2024. (Michael M. Santiago / Getty) Despite all of this, Dershowitz has arrived at a nuanced take on his snubbing. “I think it’s selective cancellation,” he told me. “We decided, basically, to change our life on the Vineyard.” He said that he keeps busy by writing and doing regular paid appearances on Newsmax, occasional hits on Fox News, Piers Morgan’s show on YouTube, and other outlets. (He used to be on CNN all the time, but no more—“CNN has canceled me.”) He said that he does not lack social options. He has become very active in a Vineyard Chabad that he helped start. He told me at one point about all of the new friends he’s made. “Most of them are more supportive of Israel than the other group was,” he said. “And I often ask myself, How did I allow myself to become part of that other group? ” When I asked Dershowitz who his new friends are, we wound up talking about someone who is definitely in the “other group”: Larry David. They used to speak all the time, Dershowitz told me. They would have dinner, share jokes. “I allowed him to use my gym to work out,” Dershowitz said. “I helped him on a number of occasions.” “Larry David doesn’t talk to me anymore,” Dershowitz said at another point. “He screams and yells at me when he sees me.” He told me that he used to be a fan of Curb Your Enthusiasm but can no longer bring himself to watch it. When discussing David, Dershowitz often spoke in the present tense, describing their breach as if it were an active feud and a still-fresh wound. Predictably, David had minimal enthusiasm for discussing any of this when I reached out to him. “﻿I don’t know why he’s still thinking and talking about me,” he told me by email. As for the five-year-old confrontation at the Chilmark store, David added this: “I have lots of confrontations on my show but rarely in life,” he said. “And then only if I think I can take them in a fight. Hence the Dershowitz dust-up.” W hile Dershowitz and I spoke on the porch, a woman sitting in a rocking chair next to him kept leaning in, almost certainly eavesdropping. She confirmed this about half an hour into our conversation. “I’m sorry to interrupt,” the woman said to Dershowitz. “I was just sitting here. And I just wanted to say, you sound super fascinating. And I hope nobody’s ever mean to you. Ever.” Dershowitz kvelled. “Did you plant her there or something?” I joked (sort of). “I only paid her 10 dollars,” he joked (I think). During our conversation, Dershowitz told me about a less cordial episode that had taken place last month in front of the Chilmark store, just a few feet from where we were sitting. The incident was not covered in the media, but Dershowitz had filmed a portion of it on his phone and shared the video with me. A guy in a Yankees cap had spotted Dershowitz at the store and promptly launched a barrage of Bronx cheers his way from the parking lot. The man showed exemplary message discipline. “Do you defend pedophiles? Do you defend pedophiles?” he repeated. “Yes, he does.” Dershowitz demanded that his tormentor identify himself. “My name is Jeffrey Epstein Jr., great friend to Alan Dershowitz,” the man replied. Dershowitz kept demanding that the man state his name. “What are you going to do?” the man asked. “I’m going to sue you if you give your name,” Dershowitz said. (Surprisingly, the man continued to withhold his name.) “Why? What are you going to sue me for?” he asked. “For defamation.” The heckler also mocked Dershowitz for, among other things, claiming to a TV reporter that, although he’d once received a massage from an adult woman at Epstein’s house, he’d kept his underwear on during the experience. “He was on the plane, and he kept his underwear on,” the man taunted, while retreating across the street. There was some more hollering back and forth. “You’re still a schmuck,” Dershowitz shouted. In the pantheon of rogues and sleazeballs that Dershowitz has represented, Epstein stands out. Dershowitz helped orchestrate the late sex offender’s controversial plea deal in 2008; Epstein was allowed to plead guilty to state prostitution crimes in Florida, but he avoided federal trafficking charges and wound up serving just 13 months in jail. (At the time of his death, in 2019, he was awaiting trial on federal charges of child sex trafficking, by which point Dershowitz had fallen out with him and was no longer representing him.) Earlier in their relationship, they were frequent companions. Dershowitz was a visitor to Epstein’s homes in Palm Beach and New York, and went once with his wife and daughter to Epstein’s infamous island. (“No young women there,” Dershowitz wrote to me by email. “No one there except staff and ghislaine Maxwell.”) I asked Dershowitz whether he’d ever been a passenger on Epstein’s plane. “Oh, 20 times,” he said. As Epstein’s attorney, he explained, when he had to travel to Florida, his client would fly him down. However, the heckler’s claim that Dershowitz had received a massage on the plane was incorrect. That had taken place at Epstein’s home in Palm Beach. “This was a shoulder-and-neck massage, from an older woman,” Dershowitz told me. He said that this was “the only massage I’ve ever had in Epstein’s situation.” “I’ve never in my life had an erotic massage. Not even from my wife,” he added, excruciatingly. Dershowitz has said repeatedly that he never witnessed or participated in any unlawful sexual impropriety related to Epstein. In 2014, the Epstein survivor Virginia Giuffre alleged in court documents that the financier had trafficked her to multiple men while she was a minor. This included Dershowitz, who vehemently denied the charges. Giuffre sued Dershowitz for defamation, and Dershowitz countersued, claiming that she had made up the accusations. Giuffre withdrew her suit against Dershowitz in 2022, acknowledging that she might have made a mistake in identifying him. She died by suicide last year. [ Gilad Edelman: What everyone assumes about Jeffrey Epstein ] “I wish I never met him,” Dershowitz told me, speaking of Epstein. “But I don’t regret my representation of him.” This struck me as a classic bit of Dershowitz hairsplitting, and I was not quite sure what to make of it. Regardless, Dershowitz conveyed far more remorse over representing Epstein than I heard him express about any of his other clients. And he told me that he is resigned to Epstein being a lasting stain on his reputation and legacy. “I’ve been already told I will have a bad obituary in The New York Times ,” he volunteered. “Who told you that?” I asked. “Do they work at The New York Times ?” “No,” Dershowitz said. He claimed to have heard it “from a guy who does obituaries for another newspaper.” (Apparently, all obit writers swap notes.) He added that an obituary writer for the Times did call him. “With his deep obituary voice,” he noted, affecting a stentorian baritone. “I have to tell you that your obituary will include the allegations against you from Jeffrey Epstein,” the Times reporter said, according to the deep-voiced Dershowitz. He said that he’d urged the obit guy to “put it in perspective.” (Danielle Rhoades Ha, a New York Times spokesperson, declined to comment on any specific obituaries but told me by email, “We don’t write ‘negative’ or ‘positive’ obituaries, but strive for fair, comprehensive and accurate accounts of a person’s full life.”) Tony Luong for The Atlantic Dershowitz wanted to make clear to me how unfair he believes the Epstein-related allegations against him are. He and his wife have been married for 40 years, he said: “I have never cheated. I have never hugged—I don’t hug people. I don’t like hugging.” He also told me that he is “not a big massage person.” “And by the way, nobody on the Vineyard believed this, even the people who hated me,” Dershowitz added. “Because they all see me with my wife.” He went further. “In fact, the lawyer for Virginia Giuffre, he came over to me one day”—it was during a deposition—“and said, ‘Alan, I’ve seen you with your wife. I can’t believe you would ever have done anything.’” I said I was dubious that the opposing lawyer would say something like this. “I’ll give you his name—his name is Chuck Cooper.” Reached by phone for comment, Charles Cooper, Giuffre’s lawyer, told me the exchange that Dershowitz had described had never taken place. “This event that he’s reporting and this comment that he’s attributing to me are both categorically untrue,” Cooper said. He added that he remembers seeing Dershowitz with his wife on only one occasion, and that it was enough for him to make only a “fleeting observation.” Either way, “I did not say and I would never have said what he’s attributed to me,” Cooper said. “Give me a break.” I n the course of my discussion with Dershowitz, I learned of another fundamental change to his life, one that filled me with something I did not expect to feel: pathos. Last year, Dershowitz’s son Elon died at 64, after suffering a stroke. He had been diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor when he was 10 and had been told that he’d be lucky to make it to his bar mitzvah. “We took extraordinary steps,” Dershowitz said, “all over the world.” Elon had been his father’s sidekick. A film producer, he was the prime mover behind Reversal of Fortune , the 1990 legal thriller based on Dershowitz’s book about his successful defense of the British socialite Claus von Bülow in his trial for the attempted murder of his wife. The film solidified the status of Dershowitz (played by Ron Silver) as one of the “super lawyers” of his generation. “We went to the Oscars together,” Dershowitz said of him and Elon. Jeremy Irons won Best Actor for his portrayal of von Bülow. They went to an after-party. “I sat next to Gregory Peck, and it was a great moment,” Dershowitz said. When Dershowitz spoke about Elon, I detected a note of anguish in his voice. On the Vineyard, they’d been pretty much inseparable. Dershowitz’s son used to join him at the Chilmark store, when he still held court. “He would come to the porch with me every day,” Dershowitz said. If anyone came up and started giving him trouble, Elon would get after them. “He was my guy.” [ Read: Nantucket doesn’t belong to the preppies ] Everybody on the Vineyard liked Elon, Dershowitz said: “Even when they turned against me, they generally didn’t turn against Elon.” “Although Larry David did.” “Even when my son died—and Larry knew him very well—he never sent me a card,” Dershowitz said. “Never called me, never did anything to acknowledge it.” After I returned from the Vineyard, I spoke with Dershowitz by phone. Since my visit, he’d suffered a fractured rib. When I asked how it had happened, he lamented that the cause was nothing dramatic. “I mean, I’d love to have a great story,” he said. “Passionate lovemaking, you know?” (Although definitely not an erotic massage.) Alas. “I sneezed too hard,” he said. “My doctor told me at my age, a sneeze or a hard cough can fracture a rib.” Despite being in pain, Dershowitz said that he was planning to go that night to a Chabad event at the home of the billionaire hedge-fund manager Paul Singer, a big Republican donor and supporter of Israel. In a few days, Dershowitz was scheduled to be honored at the Chabad to mark the 75th anniversary of his bar mitzvah. We briefly revisited the Pierogi Incident; he sent me a link to a Facebook post from someone marking “the anniversary of Pierogigate” and vowing to “have a potato pierogi later today in honor of Dershowitz.” When I mentioned Larry David’s name again, Dershowitz sounded freshly pained—as if I’d elbowed him in his bad rib. They had been really good friends, he reiterated. I asked whether he’d had any interaction with David since the Chilmark-store episode in 2021. Not really, Dershowitz said, except for one chance meeting at a restaurant, in which David had again blown him off. Later, Dershowitz wanted to know whether I’d spoken with David for this story. After our initial email exchange, I finally did speak with David by phone late last week. He was on vacation on Martha’s Vineyard, and I expected him to be cantankerous and annoyed—which he was at first. When I brought up the matter of Elon’s death, however, David’s tone shifted. “He’s 100 percent right,” David told me, referring to Dershowitz. “I should have reached out, and I certainly regret not doing so. As I said on Curb once, ‘I think of nice things. I just don’t act on them.’” David, who turned 79 last month, said that he has been “softening” and might be open to some kind of rapprochement with Dershowitz, if only to extinguish their one-way feud once and for all. “I’m starting to feel a little sorry for him, actually,” David told me. “Certainly because of his son.” It was a touching moment, and seemed sincere. But something also felt off, as if the network had enlisted focus groups and then ordered up a feel-good ending. Then David sent me an email the next morning. “I’m loath to say anything mean because he’s been so ostracized,” he wrote of Dershowitz. A reversion to sarcasm! “But he only has himself to blame. He made a deal with the devil. Literally. And I’d bet the devil hasn’t said a word to him since the impeachment.”

items.title: Islamophobia Has Corroded American Values
items.description: E very July, I take my boys back to my hometown in Indiana so we can watch the Independence Day parade. They run around in American-flag shirts and devour far too many rocket pops as vintage cars, tractors, and an Abraham Lincoln in shorts make their way down Main Street. I’ve always loved that parade, but it’s not the same one I recall watching as a girl. In recent years—in between the marching bands and Girl Scouts—comes a camouflage military Humvee, a papier-mâché bald eagle flying at a jumbo-size Bible, and a tribute to “Indiana’s fallen heroes,” during which photos of so many, too many, young Hoosiers who fought in Afghanistan and Iraq are carried out on banners. It’s a somber scene. The shadow of September 11, the wars that followed, and the culture that shaped us all hangs over the parade. I’m not usually one to read much into the symbolism of anniversaries, but this year marks both 250 years since the founding of the United States and 25 years since 9/11. I can’t think of one without the other, because September 11 not only transformed how the United States interacted with Muslims abroad and at home; it also changed our collective view of American values around citizenship, identity, and civil liberties. In my earliest memories, we didn’t have a hometown mosque—there wasn’t enough money or enough Muslims to build one. But by the early 1990s, the community had raised the funds. We were excited to celebrate our newly constructed mosque amid the cornfields, but not everyone felt the same way. During the official ground-breaking, one of the neighbors blasted music aggressively. Then one day, a mountain of dirt appeared along that neighbor’s property line—a berm to, presumably, hide the mosque from sight. We children were warned to stay away. If someone accidentally kicked a soccer ball into the neighbor’s lawn, we were not to chase it. It’s disorienting, as a kid, to feel unwelcome in your own hometown. [ Steven B. Smith: How to love the U.S.A. ] I was a teenager on September 11, and mourned with all Americans the terrible loss of 2,977 lives on that awful day. Three months later, bullet holes were discovered in a window at the mosque, though no one saw the culprit and no one was hurt. Muslim communities in other parts of the country faced more threats in the days, weeks, and years that followed. It became routine for women in hijabs to be harassed and for mosques to be vandalized. In Ohio, a man plowed his Ford Mustang into the front door of a mosque. In Texas, a man threw a Molotov cocktail toward a mosque; children fled as it shattered. In Seattle, a man attempted to set fire to cars in a mosque parking lot and then fired a gun at worshippers. I’m not sure how much I knew of these episodes at the time, but I was well aware that some Americans were deeply distrustful of Muslims, and I worried about the rumblings of government surveillance. But in my hometown, such threats were not the norm. The Indiana I grew up in was friendly, known for its “Hoosier hospitality.” Sure, it wasn’t always particularly attuned to difference. When I was in middle school, our class learned about Islam by watching Not Without My Daughter —the 1991 East-versus-West saga about an American woman, played by Sally Field, who was trapped in Iran by her husband. One of the benefits of growing up in a fairly tight-knit city with a small-town feel, though, was that a lot of folks had known me—and my siblings and parents—for most of my life. Despite the bad guys who flew airplanes into the World Trade Center, to most locals we were just “the Khalids.” I was fortunate to have a relatively normal high-school experience. For homecoming I tie-dyed my hijab red and white—our school colors—and classmates complimented the look. It sounds so much like a cheesy Hallmark movie that I’ve asked friends and family to confirm, so I can make sure I’m not misremembering it all. But as 9/11 retreats further into the past, strangely, anti-Muslim rhetoric has grown—no longer veiled or marginalized but actively celebrated by those in power. Prominent lawmakers have made it clear that they don’t see people like me as Americans. “Muslims don’t belong in American society,” Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee wrote on social media in March, the same month that Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote, “We need more Islamophobia, not less.” “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,” Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina recently posted. But the messages that are the most difficult for me to reconcile are the voices of my own people: Hoosiers. I n May, the lieutenant governor of Indiana, Micah Beckwith, went on a conservative Christian talk show and declared: “I hate Islam. It’s a demonic death cult.” (He added that he actually loves Muslims because we make “great Christians” once we find Jesus.) His comments came just days after three people were killed in a shooting at a mosque in San Diego. Beckwith didn’t mention that shooting, or any of the concerns that Muslims have for their safety—the need, for example, to hire guards or install security gates, as my old hometown mosque did. He wore a polo shirt with the insignia of the state of Indiana when he said that Americans need “permission to hate again,” and singled out Islam for that hatred. After a group of religious leaders including Jews condemned Beckwith’s comments, he called them “deeply misguided” on X and wrote, “One need not look far into history to see what happens when the sheep are persuaded they can safely coexist with the wolf.” To me, it was all a depressing sign of how much my homeland has changed in the past 25 years. I first started noticing the shift in the run-up to the 2016 election, as a reporter for NPR. I covered American politics, interviewing voters during one of the most tumultuous periods in recent politics, and an era in which being Muslim became seen as antithetical to being American. In 2015, I was at a resort in Orlando for the Florida Republican Party’s major political summit. By the time Donald Trump took the stage, the crowd was hearing murmurs of a tragedy unfolding in Paris—coordinated shootings and bombings by ISIS militants in what would become one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in French history. A Muslim woman in a hijab spotted me in the audience, and excitedly introduced herself, thinking I was a fellow Republican in this unwelcoming crowd. “Sorry, I’m a reporter,” I said. But good luck , I thought. Roughly a week later, Trump was proclaiming—falsely—that when the Twin Towers fell, “thousands and thousands” of Muslims were cheering in New Jersey. Soon after, he called for a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States until our country’s representatives can figure out what is going on.” In Florida, I met a man named Jared at an event for Trump-campaign volunteers. As I was about to leave, he stopped me. He wanted to share something that had been on his mind: why Trump’s “Muslim ban” would be beneficial for a Muslim such as me. “True believers” of Islam, he warned, have a mission: to come to the U.S. and do “heinous things.” And if they did, that would be a liability for me—I could even end up in an internment camp. A “Muslim ban,” he said, was just “risk mitigation.” I didn’t bother telling him that I had always thought of myself as a true believer: someone who prays, fasts, and believes deeply and personally in God. Shortly after that conversation, Trump casually told Anderson Cooper on CNN , “I think Islam hates us.” It was a flippant comment made by a man known for hyperbole and bombast, but one that is seared into my memory. Who exactly was “us”? Trump didn’t create suspicion of Muslims; he merely tapped into fears and distrust that had been bubbling up since 9/11. But his comments started permeating into our broader culture. In late 2018, I went to the Mahoning Valley in eastern Ohio. I’ve visited that region many times, in part because it’s a place that tells a story of changing American politics—one of the counties that voted for Barack Obama before turning redder—and in part because it reminds me of home. These are the former steel hubs, old manufacturing towns and cities where many people tell me how much better life used to be. One of my first stops was the local Republican Party headquarters, in an ordinary strip mall. Connie, one of the club’s volunteers, had told me to swing by because they were having their Christmas party that evening. Before the festivities kicked off, we were chatting, and she told me how absurd it seemed to her that classic songs like “Baby, It’s Cold Outside” had become offensive to some people. “You don’t want to hear it, go away. Get out of our country,” she said. I initially thought she was complaining in a general sense about liberals, but then the conversation turned personal. “You’re probably a Muslim?” she asked. (Probably the hijab was a giveaway.) “I don’t care for them, I’m sorry,” she continued. “First of all, take that scarf off.” “Me?” I asked, suddenly confused. “When I see girls with those headscarves on, it just irritates me,” she said. I tried to explain that I wear the scarf because I want to, that not all my sisters do, and that, frankly, my dad’s never been a big fan. “You’re so pretty,” she said—a backhanded compliment, I assumed, to convey that she just thought I’d look better without a scarf. “I mean you have a pretty face.” Connie was a former hairdresser, the kind of woman who, well into her 70s, still manicured her nails and had a blond pixie cut. I had interviewed her twice before, so perhaps that familiarity allowed her to feel that she could be candid. And I wanted to hear that candor—I was curious. So I asked her why she didn’t “care for” Muslims. “Because they want to take over America,” she said. Personally, I’d never met a Muslim who came to America to “take it over,” so I was baffled. “ Why can’t they just come here and live like us?” she went on. “If you want to be an American, be an American. Or be a Muslim.” She said it as if the two were incompatible. “Do what we do,” she continued. “We were here first, okay? You’re second.” That comment has haunted me for years: We were here first, and you’re second. T he story of Islam in America is not a foreign story; it began long before September 11—before, even, our nation’s founding. Thousands of Muslims were present in the colonies, captured in West Africa and brought to the shores of North America in chains. Historians estimate that 10 to 15 percent—possibly even 30 percent—of enslaved people transported to North America were Muslim. One of those people, Yarrow Mamout, was brought to Annapolis, Maryland, in the summer of 1752, where he was put up for sale. He spent decades enslaved on plantations in Maryland, before gaining his freedom and building a home on a plot of land he bought on what is now Georgetown. I live near where his house once stood, and to my shame knew little about Yarrow’s story, though he was so well known in his time that he was painted by the famous Revolutionary War–era portrait artist Charles Willson Peale. That portrait is now preserved at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Peale was fascinated by Yarrow and wrote about him in his diary: “Yarrow has been noted for sobriety & a chearfull conduct, he professes to be a mahometan, and is often seen & heard in the Streets singing Praises to God—and conversing with him he said man is no good unless his religion comes from the heart.” When Yarrow died in 1823, an obituary was published on him in more than 38 papers. His house is now gone, but at the site you’ll find a plaque—a reminder not just of Yarrow but of the tens of thousands of Muslims already here at the nation’s founding. When the Founders first enunciated their commitment to religious freedom, they were thinking about Muslims. The protections of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, Thomas Jefferson wrote, extended to “the Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and Mahometan, the Hindoo, and infidel of every denomination.” He invoked Islam to demonstrate the theoretical reach of religious freedom in America—even as tens of thousands of enslaved African Muslims were denied that freedom themselves. For the past three years, I’ve been working on a PBS documentary series tied to America’s 250th anniversary called American Muslims: A History Revealed that tells these and other stories. I wanted my sons to have a fuller vision of American, and Muslim, history. The 9/11 era shaped so much of my adult life. It changed not just how we deal with one another—domestic surveillance laws, TSA checks, a political shift in American partisan politics—but also how we interact with the rest of the world. I had hoped that the era of the U.S. fighting in the Middle East wouldn’t be a patriotic inheritance for my boys. But if anything, we seem to be stuck in an even worse version of 9/12—one governed less by fear than by outright hate. This unease with Islam isn’t an issue only on the right. For all of the Biden administration’s talk about diversity, few Muslims had any role in foreign-policy decisions. Many Muslim Democrats remain angry about Joe Biden’s approach to the war in Gaza, and feel that his attitude toward Palestinians abroad was so dehumanizing that it has exacerbated hostility and harassment at home. But on the right, Islamophobia has been much more direct. [ Read: What the Islamophobic attacks on Mamdani reveal ] This summer, Beckwith, the lieutenant governor of Indiana, told the podcast Conservative Review that Islam is “a more dangerous ideology than even Nazism.” I had been wondering whether he might ever apologize for saying “I hate Islam.” Eventually I emailed his office to ask. An aide replied that “Lieutenant Governor Beckwith does not regret his comments and has not had a change of heart.” Since 9/11, the Muslims of my hometown have grown in number. The mosque has expanded. I’m told that relations with the neighbor have improved, though the mound of dirt remains—now covered in grass and trees, but still a warning to stay on our side of the property line. I tried calling and texting the neighbor, but she declined to talk—replying “do I want to speak to you NO” and “you need to research your information a lot better.” Growing up, I had thought of our mosque’s neighbor as a bit of an odd character—an uncharacteristically unfriendly midwesterner, her attitude not particularly indicative of how Muslims were seen in the city or the state. But in the past decade, politicians have amplified and normalized that animosity toward Muslims, even when it has no basis in reality. This summer, Beckwith advocated for banning the Muslim call to prayer on loudspeakers—though there are no reports of any mosques in Indiana publicly broadcasting it.

items.title: A Time for Female Monsters
items.description: Most dramas about murderous women save the revelations of deviance for the end, after parceling out uncertainty and complication. Furious does things exactly backwards. Here is a monster , the Hulu series announces with its very first scene, during which an unblinking blonde in a Halloween cat mask kills a man by forcibly injecting him with fentanyl, which she keeps in a bedazzled silver tin. “I don’t really like listening to you,” she whispers, as he gasps for breath. “I don’t like the sounds you’re making. But I love your smile.” After he dies, she reaches for a bowl of candy corn, which she eats slowly and with care, piece by piece. The scene felt confrontational to me at first watch, as though it were daring me to switch it off in discomfort. But why? Crime shows begin with violated women all the time—the naked, bloodied female corpse is such a staple in the genre’s visual language that viewers hardly notice it. Why is a scene of a young woman luxuriating in her sadistic treatment of a man so unsettling? As Furious goes on, it offers up more murders, but also more context for why this woman, Catherine (played by Lola Petticrew), is doing what she’s doing—and although she remains monstrous, the show shades in her full, horrifying humanity. Furious —created by the writer Liz Meriwether and executive-produced by the actor Emmy Rossum, who also stars in it—is preoccupied with elemental ideas about violence and transformation, which juxtapose nicely with the more conventional framework of a police procedural. Rossum plays Alice, a former detective turned FBI grunt who’s dragged into investigating Catherine’s latest victim by her former partner Danny (Scoot McNairy). Like Catherine, Alice has been warped by trauma; her previous boyfriend, also a police officer (Jake Lacy), beat her, and all of her colleagues except Danny froze her out when she finally reported him. She uses apps to find sexual partners who will agree to beat her, role-playing her own abuse. In one episode, she outright refuses to shower, a tendency that seems off-putting until her sister reveals to Danny that her ex used to drag her from the shower to hit her, sometimes leaving her passed out under the running water. [ Read: Everything we know about rape is wrong ] Early on, the show evokes Medusa—whose rape at the hands of Poseidon saw her turned into a hideous Gorgon with snakes for hair—in reference to Catherine, whose own history is at least as cruel; there are also multiple references to the Furies, winged goddesses of retribution. Nora Washington (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), who runs the FBI sex-crimes division that Alice is trying to get assigned to, describes the room that agents use to review child-sexual-abuse material as “the darkest pit of Hades down deep in the bottom of the Earth.” Washington’s perpetual rage, and her attempts to quash it with emotional detachment and tequila, suffuses every scene she’s in. Watching the show, I remembered the moment, almost a decade ago, when women’s anger became the subject of countless books and news stories—when many people expressed hope that it might have a revolutionary power. Instead, during a period when women have lost fundamental rights and have been confronted with the apparent futility of their protests, cultural narratives about women’s rage no longer have the luxury of optimism. Instead, anger has metastasized into vengeance, inflamed and out for blood. While watching Furious , I happened to read Honey , by Imani Thompson: a wry and erudite take on the dark-academia genre about a Ph.D. candidate at Cambridge named Yrsa (derived from an Old Norse word for “furious”) who—almost accidentally—becomes a serial killer. Yrsa’s journey toward murder begins casually one day, when she tips a bee into the lemonade of an older male colleague who has betrayed Yrsa’s friend and stolen credit for the research project they were working on together. When the bee stings the man, who’s allergic to them, Yrsa watches while he chokes to death, observing “the theatrics of the wheezing man. The red-hot raspberry of his face.” When he falls to the ground, she gets onto her knees and strokes his hair. Afterward, she eats ice cream. Murder in the book becomes associated with sweetness and satiation. In dull moments after the man’s death, Yrsa replays the scene in her mind, and it fills her up. Thompson wanted to write about a female serial killer, she said in one interview , because “we always see the woman as a victim,” in ways that are often glamorized. But Yrsa is also working on a Ph.D. about “Afropessimism and Black women’s discourses on their liberation,” and the book is studded with references to academics and writers who consider the heritage of violence. Yrsa often uses critical theory to try to justify what she’s doing: She cites thinkers such as Audre Lorde, Stuart Hall, and Saidiya Hartman, and fixates particularly on Hartman’s essay Venus in Two Acts , about all of the nameless murdered Black girls obliterated by history. How, Hartman wonders, can she “revisit the scene of subjection without replicating the grammar of violence?” In Yrsa’s mind, this question becomes twisted into the idea that punishing abusive men might redress some of the imbalance. Yrsa does so in part by tracking down men outed on a site where sex workers name their most vicious clients. She injects one with a fatal dose of heroin and enjoys doing it, much like Catherine, savoring the memory of “that moment when she realized he was vulnerable only to her. That moment when she could do anything.” Late in Furious , Catherine tells Alice about how her brutal actions feel to her: “It’s power, watching someone die.” She adds, “When I’m killing someone, it’s like I’m eating him, like I’m swallowing him, like everything he’s ever done is disappearing inside me.” She is, it turns out, pursuing and murdering the men who hurt her when she was an underage teenager being trafficked for sex, starting with the pimp who beat, raped, and starved her. Her pleasure in killing, unlike Yrsa’s, is derived not from the act itself but from neutralizing what these men did to her. [ Read: When women are accused of complicity ] The show is a fascinating pivot for Meriwether, who previously created the beloved offbeat Fox comedy New Girl and who most recently co-created the FX series Dying for Sex , about a woman who receives a fatal cancer diagnosis and decides to pursue sexual pleasure in her final months. There are moments in Furious that come off as morbidly comic—an FBI agent played by Rob Yang shouts “Boom!” at inopportune moments, and a witness with muscular dystrophy (Steve Way) needles police officers with his wheelchair—but more often, the series is pitch-dark. The show was shot with anamorphic lenses to foster a moody, surveillant feeling, evoking David Fincher more than Law & Order: Special Victims Unit . The point seems to be to use the visual language of neo-noir while shifting the focus to characters who don’t usually draw the camera’s attention. Furious has been referred to as a “crime drama for a post-Epstein world,” and one of the characters—a billionaire with similar proclivities who seems to operate with impunity—seems modeled after the serial sex offender. “The ones who are really to blame don’t get caught, never, never,” Nora tells Alice. “You think you’re ever gonna catch anyone who matters?” But Meriwether, in an interview with Vulture , noted that she was “much more interested in the experience of the women than I am with the experience of the perpetrator,” and the show is especially curious regarding women who become compelled to victimize others. What does living with that kind of trauma and injustice do to a person’s psyche? “My memory sucks ,” Catherine says in one scene, trying to piece together fragments of her past life into a coherent shape. “It’s ’cause I got strangled so much.” The actors in Furious are uniformly brilliant: Bernstine’s achingly blasé Nora; McNairy’s frowsy, compassionate Danny; Rossum’s magnetic and volatile Alice. Petticrew turns Catherine’s postured immaturity into something vividly repulsive—she’s constantly restaging the girlhood she never got to have, but in an unavoidably corrupted way. By the show’s end, we can better understand her, even if we’re lucky enough not to have her tolerance for cruelty. What happens to anger when it can’t be absorbed? We can only consider whether there’s truth in Nora’s assertion that only evil can really fight evil, and that in order to defend humanity, you occasionally have to sacrifice your own. ​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: Jason Arday’s Final Self-Delusion
items.description: In the Henrik Ibsen play The Wild Duck , Dr. Relling dispenses a drug that soothes the most profound self-loathing: livsløgn , a “life-lie,” a form of grandiose self-delusion that lets the pathetic figures who take it believe that they are geniuses and noble romantics. The life-lie, it turns out, is a hell of a drug—perhaps the most potent Scandinavian pharmaceutical invention before Ozempic—and keeps the play’s fragile characters from succumbing to “self-contempt and despair.” Against Relling’s advice, another character, Gregers, decides to free these losers from their life-lies and expose them. The play ends with a suicide. On Friday, the former Cambridge professor Jason Arday died at the age of 41. British police said his death was “unexpected” but not “suspicious.” This classification, unexpected but not suspicious , includes the possibility that he died accidentally. But reports of Arday’s delicate emotional state at the time have led most to assume that he killed himself after weeks of accumulating revelations that he had lied compulsively for personal and professional gain. One of his last public statements was an interview with The Times of London in which he affirmed that he was “not a liar,” a line itself so blatantly false that any Ibsen fan would have recognized symptoms of a livsløgn overdose. He gave no George Santos–like, impish shrug at having been finally caught. ( What took you so long? ) He did not prepare to switch careers to pursue reality-TV stardom or write a Catch Me if You Can –style memoir about the dupes he met along the way. Instead, his response suggested—it is painful to notice this now, when nothing can be done—that he felt he had to stick with his story. That way led to a catastrophic end: narcissistic collapse, in which the lies stop working on others and finally on the liar himself. Arday appears to have convinced himself, wrongly, that the last remaining option was suicide, which was, of course, his final self-delusion. His lies won him undeserved praise and status, and they gave (unforgivably) false hope to people whose loved ones have severe developmental delays. But the only lie that ever killed anyone was the last one. Some are now suggesting that Arday was the victim, and the people who drew attention to his lies, the villains. Ibram X. Kendi suggests that Arday might even be vindicated after a full accounting of the allegations against him. (Keep in mind that in addition to his straightforward acts of fabrication and plagiarism, always of less powerful academics, he claimed to have taken part in a British documentary series that preceded his birth.) And the hapless Good Law Project, which persuaded dozens of Cambridge bigwigs to rally behind Arday and dismiss his critics as racists, has issued an open letter calling for an investigation of “the press.” The media’s alleged crime: writing about this extraordinary case of a habitual liar’s appointment to a distinguished academic post, rather than letting the liar keep embarrassing himself and his institution. “Reasonable public interest” in the case had dissipated, the letter says, yet the press kept digging. Arday’s death was, it says, the “direct, foreseeable and foreseen result of press harassment.” A Buddhist proverb says that when a wise man points at the moon, the fool stares at his finger. The media were unrelenting, but con-man stories are always popular, and the bigger the victim, the better. The press’s obsession was in proportion with the outlandishness of the lies told by Arday and on his behalf, and with public interest in the failures they revealed. Those failures were intellectual, institutional, and even legal. Arday called the cops on an academic who had asked him hostile questions, and he instructed a law firm to send a threatening letter to a reporter who did the same. The focus on those who pointed out Arday’s shortcomings, rather than on Arday himself and those who abetted his rise, is a clear sign that lessons from this miserable episode remain unlearned. The people responsible for it may repeat their errors and, in some cases, commit appalling new ones. (Kendi compares Arday’s treatment to a “lynching.” This analogy is tenable only if you think lynching means harshly criticizing people for actual transgressions, rather than summarily murdering them for no reason at all.) [ Read: The truths that failed Jason Arday ] Some lies are so preposterous that intelligent people who believe them bear some responsibility for being taken in. And they are outright guilty for repeating the lies and urging others to believe them. This is obviously so in Arday’s case. The lies depended on willful credulity, as well as amplification by other professors, including Cambridge’s Hilary Cremin, who went on the BBC and told Arday that “you are the best in the world, in terms of the research that you do.” Reviewers gushed over his books and pronounced them moving, “brave,” and “insightful.” Defenders did begin to distance themselves when the lies became even more lurid and inexplicable, as with the claims that a masked man invisible to security cameras had menaced Arday with a knife and that someone had sent him the head of a pig, which he disposed of rather than preserved as evidence. The trajectory of his deception seems to have been from tragedy (a man carried away with lies and too compulsive to stop telling them) to farce (once the lies became ridiculous enough that only a complicit person could believe them) and finally back to tragedy on Friday. Arday’s colleagues, his editors, and the people who knew he was a fraud but said nothing have absorbed some ridicule for their role in hiring and publishing him. But to date, I have seen no evidence that they have considered their complicity, let alone repaired the damage to their institutions by explaining their error or, better yet, just resigning . They elevated Arday, a fragile and disturbed person, into a position where his fragility would be tested and he would be shattered. Even if the Cambridge Faculty of Education’s standards were so low that his inadequacies would remain unremarked there, he was a fellow of a Cambridge college with real scholars who would eventually be indignant upon realizing that their new colleague’s scholarship consisted of copy-paste jobs, semiliterate nonsense, and fan notes on his favorite 1990s Brit-pop. Did Arday’s allies think no one would notice? That those who noticed would be forever intimidated into polite silence? That drinking sherry in the common room of Jesus College would be a pleasant experience for Arday himself as he waited to be found out? Those who placed Arday in that situation were cruel and heartless. They may as well have taken a skin-and-bones Make-A-Wish kid, told him that he could fly, and shot him out of a cannon. The journalists were not the ones who stuffed Arday into the cannon and lit the fuse. They were gravity. In The Wild Duck , Ibsen’s main villain is Gregers, the crusading moralist who makes it his mission to “rescue” the characters from their sustaining life-lies and help them and those who respect them see their deficiencies. The Gregers in this case is Nathan Cofnas, a philosopher with an abiding interest in race and a particular curiosity about the supposed mental deficiencies of Black people. Cofnas’s views on race science (he believes that very few Black people are cognitively equipped to be employed at a “meritocratic” university) led him to be run out of Cambridge in 2024, just as Arday was being appointed to one of the university’s most prestigious chairs. Cambridge’s failure to vet this appointment left an opening for Cofnas, smarting from his own dismissal, to take on the unsavory task of assembling a dossier on Arday’s work. The results were so galling that morbid curiosity drove others to scrutinize everything else about Arday, including his implausible claims that he secretly raised large sums for charity and was among the world’s greatest long-distance runners. [ Read: Icarus in the faculty lounge ] Dr. Relling calls Gregers’s urge to disabuse and expose “an acute attack of integrity,” and he warns that going cold turkey off livsløgn will not end well for patients or others. (Other Ibsen plays are relevant here too: In some, the collapse of illusions afflicts whole towns, not just a few of their members.) The difference between Gregers and Cofnas seems to be that the latter, perhaps as a result of his being scorned by Cambridge, has no affection for the people whose life-lies he methodically destroyed. Cofnas recently told the podcaster Winston Marshall that “talking about” race “makes people feel bad, and there are a lot of things that are true that make people feel bad that we don’t need to talk about.” But the subversion of academic standards, at what Cofnas perceives as his own expense, demanded action. The result will be good for academia, Cofnas insists, a far better outcome than preserving the good feelings that went along with silence. In Ibsen, when Gregers forces integrity on a self-deluded character, that character’s daughter decides to kill herself. Gregers sounds most like Cofnas in the final scene. He is confident that her death, however horrible, will “set free all that is noble” in those who partook in the life-lie as they see life for what it is. Life sustained by delusion “is not worth living,” Gregers says. But he knows the cost of being an odious truth teller. “I am glad that my destiny is what it is,” he tells Relling: “to be the thirteenth at table,” the guest who everyone wishes would stop showing up, because he brings misfortune to any dinner he attends. Arday was hired to teach social science. A terminal irony is that his main contribution to that body of knowledge will be as a case study, about a community that elevated a flawed man to a position exalted beyond his ability, without knowing or caring that they were actually offering him as a human sacrifice.

items.title: Trump Is Putting His Face on Everything
items.description: W e Americans remember our presidents in all sorts of ways, with monuments and statues, on coins and street signs. Another thing we do is wait—we wait until a president is safely out of office, or dead, before we bestow such honors. Donald Trump has bent many democratic traditions, but this one, he’s discarded altogether. Trump has been putting his name on buildings since before most Americans were born. He built his political career atop his personal brand, and much of his second term has been defined by an obsession with leaving his mark . The result is something entirely new in the nation’s history. The more you look, the more you see Trump’s face, name, or signature all around you—on a government building, infrastructure project, banknote, taxpayer-funded website, or official document. COMPLETED Trump’s face has appeared swiftly , often with little warning—and nowhere more so than in the nation’s capital . To find a comparable leader so fixated on the proliferation of his image, the historians I spoke with reached across oceans and time: The face of Hafez al-Assad, who ruled Syria for nearly three decades, was printed on children’s schoolbook covers; Mussolini covered Rome’s Palazzo Braschi with a display featuring his head . Obviously Mao Zedong comes to mind. This creation of a cult of personality is partly how strongmen have sought to erase memories of their predecessors and “insert themselves into the social fabric,” Ruth Ben-Ghiat, a historian of authoritarianism at NYU, told me. There may not be a perfect comparison, but past regimes offer clues, the scholars said, about how a leader’s ubiquity can help inure citizens to broader shifts in their relationship to their government. Kevin Carter / Getty Trump’s face—staring back at federal workers, residents, and tourists from banners draped on agencies such as the Labor Department—sends a message that “he is inseparable from these more impersonal institutions of governance,” says Lisa Wedeen, a political scientist at the University of Chicago. Kevin Carter / Getty A banner featuring the president’s face appeared on the Agriculture Department ( right ) last year, but was taken down soon after. Banners similar to it remain on the Labor, Justice ( left ), and Interior ( center ) Departments, despite objections by Democrats over the cost and the message they send—especially at the Justice Department , which, particularly since Watergate, has tried to operate autonomously from the president, for all sorts of obvious reasons. Anna Moneymaker / Getty The U.S. Institute of Peace, a government-funded think tank, had Donald J. Trump added to its name in December, even as a battle over the administration’s efforts to take control of the institute continues to play out in court. Kevin Dietsch / Getty The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts likewise has become the target of a Trump takeover. The center, initially named the National Cultural Center, was renamed for Kennedy through an act of Congress two months after his assassination. Kevin Carter / Getty Less than six months after loyalists Trump installed on the center’s board put his name on the center’s facade, the lettering came down following a judge’s order. But two months later, a tarp continues to cover the spot where the president’s name once was—and the board now wants to inscribe this on the facade: Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump . Andrew Leyden / Getty In a rush to “beautify” Washington, D.C., the president has turned stretches of the city into a construction zone —in part by redirecting money once used for national-park repairs. The most notable among these beautification efforts involves the Reflecting Pool and launched a thousand headlines this summer, as fresh sealant flaked off and algae bloomed. Saul Loeb / AFP / Getty Although every president brings his own interior-decorating sense to the People’s House, Trump has dramatically altered the building’s appearance. At least three paintings and one statue at the White House illustrate the moments following the July 2024 attempt on Trump’s life in Butler, Pennsylvania. Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Chip Somodevilla / Getty Demetrius Freeman / The Washington Post / Getty Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Andrew Harnik / Getty Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux Trump has filled the White House with portraits of himself. One painting is positioned between official portraits of former First Ladies Laura Bush and Hillary Clinton. Another, which is hanging in the West Wing, depicts him, Henry Clay, and Abraham Lincoln with the label The Tariff Men . Yet another shows Trump with Lincoln and Ronald Reagan. Celal Gunes / Anadolu / Getty Late last year, the White House unveiled a “Presidential Walk of Fame” in the colonnade connecting the West Wing to the White House residence. Gold plaques and framed images of past presidents, including an autopen in place of President Biden, are examples of the administration’s attempts to rewrite history—in Trump’s signature color , no less. Travel.state.gov / U.S. Department of State As part of the celebration of America’s 250th birthday this year, the administration released what it calls the “Patriot Passport”—a special commemorative document featuring Trump’s face. The State Department began issuing the passports in July to those applying in person at the Washington, D.C., passport agency. National Park Service This year’s $80 annual resident National Parks pass looks quite different from those issued in years past (think: misty redwoods, a camouflaging frog, a snowy mountainside). Now it features Trump’s face beside George Washington’s. An environmental group sued, arguing that the Interior Department had violated a law requiring the passes to display the winner of an annual public-lands photo contest. trumpcard.gov Trump has made mass deportation a pillar of his domestic agenda, but the Trump Gold Card offers a special residency permit to foreigners willing to make a $1 million “contribution” to the United States. (Only one person is said to have received the card thus far.) A government website claims that a Trump Platinum Card is coming soon—offering up tax-related benefits in exchange for $5 million. Officials have said the funds collected through the visas will be directed to the Treasury Department. Brendan Smialowski / AFP / Getty Trump’s name made its way into the “.gov” URL for the site advertising the administration’s child-savings-account program —as well as to the top of the official IRS form that applicants must fill out. trumprx.gov ; trumpira.gov ; trumpaccounts.gov Two other government websites similarly bear Trump’s name: TrumpRx deals with prescription-drug costs and launched in February; TrumpIRA advertises a federal platform for retirement savings, and is set to roll out in 2027. nps.gov Trump celebrated his 80th birthday on June 14 with a UFC fight on the White House’s South Lawn. Other Americans could celebrate the occasion at national parks: The Interior Department deemed it a “resident-only patriotic fee-free” day. @realDonaldTrump / Truth Social This spring, the Treasury Department announced that Trump’s signature would appear on future bills—a first for a sitting president. U.S. Treasurer Brandon Beach, the official who oversees the production of coins and paper money, called the move “not only appropriate, but also well deserved.” Saul Loeb / AFP / Getty A major promise of Trump’s first presidential campaign, the border wall—which remains under construction —includes plaques featuring his signature. Chandan Khanna / AFP / Getty George Walker IV / AP Andrew Caballero-Reynolds / AFP / Getty Amy Beth Bennett / South Florida Sun-Sentinel / TNS / Getty Elsewhere around the country, local officials have pushed for naming streets and highways after the president. Although the majority of those measures have so far gone nowhere, a few came to fruition. A Trump bridge was unveiled in Tennessee last month, and Palm Beach International Airport was renamed for the president. Trump’s sons were passengers on the first flight to land at the freshly renamed airport. Helen H. Richardson / MediaNews Group / The Denver Post / Getty Last March, Trump deemed a portrait of himself that had been hanging in the Colorado state capitol since 2019 “purposefully distorted.” Lawmakers voted to “immediately” remove the unflattering picture. Thomas Peipert / AP A few months later, the president celebrated the portrait that took its place. The artist, Vanessa Horabuena, says she drove 33 hours in two days that summer to hand-deliver another one of her paintings to the White House. IN THE WORKS The Kennedy Center debacle offered the president a reminder: “Letters can easily be taken off of the surface of buildings,” Lawrence Vale, an MIT urban-planning professor who studies capital-city design and national identity, told me. Come 2029, if a Democrat wins back the White House, it’s difficult to imagine the Trump-faced banners and paintings remaining up for long. Other things—multimillion-dollar monuments, travel documents, money in circulation—would be far more challenging to undo. CFA (Commission of Fine Arts) It’s not in the official name, but everyone can plainly see—it’s the Arc de Trump. Jim Bourg / Redux Andrew Harnik / Getty Inspired by Napoleon’s Arc de Triomphe, the prospective arch has faced backlash from locals worried that the 250-foot-tall monument would ruin the city’s skyline and tarnish the sacred stretch that connects the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery. The arch is still in the planning stage, but the president has shared various models with donors. Salwan Georges / The Washington Post / Getty Trump has dismissed the idea of the “President Donald J. Trump Ballroom” as “fake news.” But a list of the project’s donors referred to it as such, and top White House officials have reportedly used the name too. McCreary Architects PLLC 2025 / whitehouse.gov Regardless of its formal title, a completed ballroom where the East Wing stood a short while ago would represent the fruition of one of the president’s biggest passion projects—and, invariably, remain associated with his name. AP Graphic / Treasury Department In the history of empires, dictators spreading their likeness via gold coin is not particularly novel. In the history of the United States, a sitting president last appeared on a coin 100 years ago, when Calvin Coolidge was featured alongside George Washington on a commemorative half-dollar issued for the nation’s 150th birthday. Last month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the U.S. Mint would soon begin producing a $1 gold-colored coin with Trump’s face on it. Kent Nishimura / AFP / Getty The Donald J. Trump $250 Bill Act proposes featuring the president on a new $250 bill. The legislation is unlikely to make it out of committee, as federal law says only portraits of deceased individuals may appear on U.S. currency. (Although living people have appeared on commemorative coins like the one Bessent announced, no living person has been featured on paper money since that statute was enacted 160 years ago.) But Beach, the treasurer, reportedly asked for prototypes of the $250 note, prompting the departure of the Treasury’s printing director. She wrote to her colleagues: “The buck stopped here.” Andrew Caballero-Reynolds / AFP / Getty The Navy’s plans for a new fleet of 15 Trump-class battleships were announced in December. But the project is still a long way off. Earlier this month, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the first of the warships would take at least eight years to build—and that the program could cost $275 billion. US Air Force The Air Force, meanwhile, in a nod to Trump—the 47th president—awarded a contract to Boeing in March to develop “the world’s first sixth-generation fighter aircraft,” to be called the F-47. “It’s a beautiful number,” Trump said when announcing the plans for the new jets. ON TRUMP’S WISH LIST Trump—and those in his orbit looking to flatter him —will almost certainly propose more places for his name and face to appear. The president could grow dissatisfied with having his name on just one airport, especially one that serves fewer than 10 million people a year. Or the new football stadium coming to Washington might grab his attention. And, of course, there is his obsession with being on Mount Rushmore. Many ideas that seemed improbable when they were first introduced have since been carried out. @realDonaldTrump / Truth Social The first time Kristi Noem met Trump in the Oval Office, she was a congresswoman from South Dakota, and he told her: “Do you know it’s my dream to have my face on Mount Rushmore?” she recounted in a 2018 interview. She remembered laughing in response; the president wasn’t laughing. On a recent trip to the monument, the president and his guests were served cookies on Air Force One that featured five presidents on the mountain, with Trump sketched in to the right of Lincoln. Courtesy Washington Commanders Last fall, ESPN reported , Trump was telling people privately that he wants the planned new Commanders stadium in D.C. to be named after him. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wouldn’t confirm the rumor, but she did tell the outlet, “That would be a beautiful name.” Courtesy Dulles Airport The airports named after John F. Kennedy (in New York), Ronald Reagan (near D.C.), and George H. W. Bush (in Houston) may be serving as inspiration. (Never mind, of course, that each of those airports was renamed after each president had died or left office.) As Dulles Airport, in Northern Virginia, prepares for a major renovation, Trump has told people that he wants the international hub renamed after him, ABC News reported; there’s a bill ready to be resuscitated that would do just that. T he tenures of previous world leaders obsessed with imparting their images onto history have yielded troves of artifacts—and left successors with the question of what to do with them all. As Hungary’s Communist era came to an end, the government confronted one such quandary. Budapest’s new government didn’t want to melt statues down or discard them, so in 1993, it deposited dozens of them in a park 20 minutes outside the city center. In one sense, the park became an oversize storage unit for junk the Hungarian public no longer needed; in another, it was a tourist attraction in its own right—a memorial to the way that a past regime had sought to memorialize itself. items.title: Trump Is at Odds With His Own Administration—And With Reality
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. A memorandum of understanding between Iran and the United States, reached in June and intended to provide breathing room to end the conflict between the two countries, expired today. The agreement will be little missed: A cease-fire had effectively ended within about three weeks of its signing, and the MOU had failed to produce fruitful negotiations or a real opening of the Strait of Hormuz. The president’s actions in the days leading up to the deadline demonstrate that his approach to the world, always contingent and improvisational, has lost its last shred of coherence. The White House cannot agree on the goals of the Iran war, much less on how to achieve them. The president is clashing with long-standing allies, in conflict with his vice president on the aims of the war, and publicly at odds with uniformed commanders over conditions for American troops stationed abroad. Trump on Friday called on Americans to accept higher gasoline prices as the cost of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. He posted this morning that the “number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon”—even though his administration assessed before the war that Iran was not actively building weapons, even though the White House hasn’t offered any explanation for how the war will prevent the regime from restarting its weapons program, and even though the war may make Iran’s desire for a nuclear arsenal only more urgent. Meanwhile, Vice President Vance says that lowering fuel prices is actually now “goal No. 1” of the war . In practice, the real aim of any diplomatic or military action now is resuming ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran seized early in the conflict—a risk foreseen by many analysts but not by Trump. For weeks now, Trump’s basic choice has been clear: Either launch a much larger military operation, including ground troops, or else surrender de facto control of the strait permanently. The president refuses to accept this. He continues to complain that the Iranians are bad-faith negotiators, which is surely true but was well known before the war. During a speech on Friday, Trump said that “pretty soon, I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.” This is dishonest, delusional, or both. Such a declaration would contradict Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s insistence on the neutrality of the strait as well as Trump’s repeated statements that the U.S. should not act as a global policeman . But it’s also beside the point, because the United States has no means to control the strait. The conditions for those U.S. troops already in the region are reportedly awful. Aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been at sea for nearly nine months, sailors report shortages of basic supplies, malfunctioning systems, and faltering mental health. When Trump was asked Friday about service members’ families who have publicly voiced their worries, he insisted that they were not concerned: “No, they’re not,” he said, adding that the ship’s deployment had not gone on “nearly long enough” yet. In a sign that military brass takes these worries seriously, the admiral overseeing the war visited the carrier this weekend and acknowledged mental-health issues. With the U.S. unwilling or unable to break the Hormuz deadlock, Oman has embarked on negotiations with Iran to create a toll system for ships. This morning, Trump threatened to expand the war with strikes against that country. “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” he told Fox News . Trump’s frustration with Oman is understandable, yet a threat to attack a venerable regional ally is still shocking. This kind of public conflict with allies has become typical. Over the weekend, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner—who has no official government post—met with Hamas officials in an attempt to revitalize an administration plan to disarm the group and rebuild Gaza. That plan is struggling for several reasons, including a flat rejection from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long been close to Trump and reportedly talked him into the Iran war. Meanwhile, Trump announced yesterday that he was curtailing joint military exercises with South Korea, “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea.” This supposed friendship has produced a splashy 2018 summit and flattering correspondence that Trump purloined from the White House after he lost the 2020 election, but it has done nothing to advance American interests. Most important, it has done nothing to curtail North Korea’s nuclear program. At the same time that Trump is fighting a war in Iran that he claims will prevent nuclear proliferation, he’s bestowing a favor on North Korea, which has offered no concessions and many threats . But Trump also gave another reason for his snub, noting that South Korea—like every other major U.S. ally—has declined to get involved in the Iran quagmire. Throughout Trump’s two terms, many analysts have sought to discern some sort of guiding doctrine to his foreign policy. The incoherence of his actions in the past week alone should provide further evidence that looking for a framework is futile. Earlier this year, my colleagues Missy Ryan and Ashley Parker reported that the White House’s foreign-affairs philosophy was “ Fuck around and find out .” Administration officials meant this as a warning to the leaders of other countries. But as the current crisis festers, they, too, are finding out. Related: The fuck-around-and-find-out presidency Trump will make South Korea pay for his Iran humiliation. Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : Julia Curlee: “The Trump White House needed me—until the fact that I am trans became public.” Jonathan Chait on what Trump officials mean by “never” Even college students have stopped hanging out. NATO’s nightmare Today’s News A 60-day window for the United States and Iran to negotiate an end to the war expired today without a final agreement . The June framework laid out terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, easing some financial restrictions on Iran, and addressing its nuclear program, but talks have stalled as both sides have traded attacks and accusations of violations. Jared Kushner met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem to discuss President Trump’s plan for Gaza after Israel said it refuses to pull back its military from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms. The Supreme Court declined for a second time to review Trump’s appeal of a $5 million civil judgment awarded to E. Jean Carroll . A federal jury in 2023 found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming Carroll; Trump paid the $5 million award last month. Dispatches The Wonder Reader : Isabel Fattal explores what the last weeks of summer can offer . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic. Source: Buyenlarge / Getty. The Problem With Child-Led Potty Training By Stephanie H. Murray The time has come to admit it: The United States has a potty-training problem. In Utah, a law came into effect last year mandating that, with some exceptions, children will not be allowed to enroll in public school without first being toilet trained. Kansas lawmakers introduced a similar bill in January, and at least one district in Florida is considering a policy change that could force kindergartners to stay home until they are out of diapers. These directives have come about because growing numbers of children are showing up to school unprepared to use the toilet. And U.S. schools aren’t the only ones confronting this issue … The shift toward delayed potty training, I learned while reporting this article, has been under way for quite a long time. Read the full article. More From The Atlantic Radio Atlantic : The Trump administration wanted her expertise, just not her. Why Lindsay Clancy’s insanity defense might fail Why learn something that a machine can do for you? How Trump left America vulnerable to cyberattacks David Frum on Trump’s last loyal constituency Culture Break Illustration by Paul Spella / The Atlantic. Sources: Getty; Shutterstock. Watch. The masked web-slinger has been setting box-office records for decades , even as the popularity of superhero movies wanes, David Sims writes. And this summer’s new Spider-Man sequel (out now in theaters) has broken nearly every record imaginable. Explore. Poetry critics didn’t always think much of Mary Oliver, whose work could sometimes read like self-help—but they didn’t give her enough credit , Hillary Kelly argues. Play our daily crossword. Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: What Trump Officials Mean by ‘Never’
items.description: Attorney General Todd Blanche has made abundantly clear that he will not act independently of President Trump’s desires. So yesterday, NBC’s Kristen Welker posed an obvious question to Blanche on Meet the Press : “If the president asks you to do something that you feel crosses an ethical or legal line, would you do it?” Blanche replied confidently, “The president will never ask me to do something unethical or illegal. He never has. He never will.” This particular formulation— never has, never will —has become a new mantra for the administration.
